Probability

Part I

Assume the distribution is known; the sample is unknown.

Basic Concepts

Counting, sets, conditioning and Bayes

Probability of an Event

Divide the number of outcomes in the event by the total number of possible outcomes.

\[P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \frac{\#\ \text{ways } \color{#93C54B}{A} \text{ can happen}}{\#\ \text{of things that can happen}} = \frac{|\color{#93C54B}{A}|}{|\Omega|}\]

Flip a coin twice

\(\Omega = \{hh,\ ht,\ th,\ tt\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{4 in all}}\)

At least one head

\(\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{hh,\ ht,\ th\} \qquad P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{3}{4} = 75\%\)

No heads

\(\color{#325D88}{B} = \{tt\} \qquad P(\color{#325D88}{B}) = \tfrac{1}{4} = 25\%\)

Roll two dice

\(\Omega = \{11,\ 12,\ \ldots,\ 66\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{36 in all}}\)

At least one five

\(\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{15, 25, 35, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 65\}\)

\(P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{11}{36}\)

Or split on the first die

\(P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{5}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{6}{36} + \tfrac{5}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}\)

Adding 6 + 6 = 12 counts the outcome (5, 5) twice. In the calculation on the right, the second case excludes a five on the first die, so the cases do not overlap.

Combinatorics and the Factorial

There are \(n\) choices and you are taking \(r\) of them. The formula depends on whether you sample with replacement and whether order matters.

\[n! = n \times (n-1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1 \qquad 0! = 1\]

With replacement Order matters

\[n^{\,r}\]

Ten coin flips in a row

\(2^{10} = 1{,}024\)

Without replacement Order matters Permutation · \(^{n}P_{r}\)

\[\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\]

Five cards off the top of the deck

\(\begin{array}{@{}r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{}} \dfrac{52!}{47!} & = & 52 \times 51 \times 50 \times 49 \times 48 \\[3pt] & = & 311{,}875{,}200 \end{array}\)

Without replacement Order does not matter Combination · \(^{n}C_{r}\)

\[\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!} = \dbinom{n}{r}\]

Different orders of the same hand

K Q 2 3 7K 2 Q 7 3

\(\dbinom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960\)

The last two formulas differ by \(r!\), the number of possible orders of the \(r\) selected items. There are 311,875,200 ordered deals and 2,598,960 hands, because each hand can be dealt in \(5! = 120\) ways.

Choosing Without Order

How many selections are possible? Order does not matter in these four examples, so each uses combinations of \(r\) items from \(n\).

chCases = [
  {q: "6 shirts, pack 3", groups: [{tag: "T", n: 6, r: 3}], what: "T-shirts"},
  {q: "10 people, call 3", groups: [{tag: "P", n: 10, r: 3}], what: "people to call"},
  {q: "8 friends, invite 4", groups: [{tag: "F", n: 8, r: 4}], what: "friends"},
  {q: "2 men + 2 women", groups: [{tag: "M", n: 5, r: 2}, {tag: "W", n: 3, r: 2}], what: "guests"}
]
viewof chIn = Inputs.form({
  q: Inputs.radio(chCases.map(d => d.q), {value: chCases[0].q, label: "Question"}),
  again: Inputs.button("Another pick")
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="cl-dials">${ins.q}${ins.again}</div>`})
chCase = chCases.find(d => d.q === chIn.q)
chC = (n, r) => { let c = 1; for (let k = 1; k <= r; k++) c = c * (n - r + k) / k; return c; }
chPick = { chIn.again;   // a fresh random pick on every press
  return chCase.groups.map(g => new Set(d3.shuffle(d3.range(g.n)).slice(0, g.r))); }
chFact = (n, r) => d3.range(n, n - r, -1).join(" × ")
chTotal = chCase.groups.reduce((t, g) => t * chC(g.n, g.r), 1)
{
  const rows = chCase.groups.map((g, gi) => html`<div class="ch-row">${d3.range(g.n).map(i =>
    html`<span class="ch-chip ${chPick[gi].has(i) ? "on" : ""}">${g.tag}${i + 1}</span>`)}</div>`);
  const one = g => html`<sup>${g.n}</sup>C<sub>${g.r}</sub> = ${g.n}! / (${g.r}! · ${g.n - g.r}!) = (${chFact(g.n, g.r)}) / (${chFact(g.r, g.r)}) = <b>${chC(g.n, g.r)}</b>`;
  const eq = chCase.groups.length === 1 ? one(chCase.groups[0])
    : html`<sup>5</sup>C<sub>2</sub> × <sup>3</sup>C<sub>2</sub> = ${chC(5, 2)} × ${chC(3, 2)} = <b>${chTotal}</b>`;
  const fb = chCase.groups.length === 1
    ? html`The selection shown is <b>one of ${chTotal}</b>. Press <b>Another pick</b> to choose different ${chCase.what}. Dividing by ${chCase.groups[0].r}! accounts for the possible orders of each selection.`
    : html`Choose the men and the women <b>separately, then multiply</b>: each of the ${chC(5, 2)} pairs of men can go with each of the ${chC(3, 2)} pairs of women, so ${chC(5, 2)} × ${chC(3, 2)} = ${chTotal}.`;
  return html`<div class="ch-wrap">${rows}<div class="ojs-eq ch-eq">${eq}</div><div class="quiz-fb">${fb}</div></div>`;
}

Sample Spaces and Events

The board shows all possible outcomes of rolling two dice. Together they form the sample space \(\Omega\). An event is a subset of these outcomes.

When outcomes are equally likely, calculate probability as a ratio of counts. \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A})\) is the cells in \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\) over the cells in \(\Omega\). That assumption holds for two fair dice, but often fails in real problems.

Unions, Intersections and Complements

The board shows two events, \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\) and \(\color{#325D88}{B}\). Their union \(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}\) is “either”, their intersection \(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}\) is “both”, and the complement \(\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}\) is every outcome left over.

Add 6 and 18 and you get 24, which is three too many. The cells in both events were counted twice, so subtract them once.

Venn diagrams

A Venn diagram shows the same events as regions inside circles. The four regions contain the same counts as the board, totalling 36.

These circles are drawn to scale, so \(\color{#325D88}{B}\) covers three times the area of \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\). Most are not, which is why the counts written on them matter more than the picture.

Set Notation for Probability

Counting gives \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = |\color{#93C54B}{A}|/|\Omega|\) and \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}) = 1 - P(\color{#93C54B}{A})\). For unions and intersections, use the following rules.

Either · \(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}\)

\[\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}} P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) - P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})\\[4pt] \phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if mutually exclusive}} \end{array}\]

Both · \(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}\)

\[\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}} P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B} \mid \color{#93C54B}{A})\\[4pt] \phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if independent}} \end{array}\]

Mutually exclusive means \(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B} = \varnothing\), so there is nothing to subtract. Independent means learning \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\) tells you nothing about \(\color{#325D88}{B}\), as the conditional probability formula shows.

Conditional Probabilities

Given that \(\color{#325D88}{B}\) occurred, restrict the sample space to its outcomes. The conditional probability is the proportion of those outcomes that also belong to \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\).

\[P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = \frac{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})}{P(\color{#325D88}{B})}\]

Independent events \(\color{#325D88}{B}\) is “the second die is a five”

Six outcomes remain, and one has a three on the first die, so \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B}) = \tfrac{1}{6}\), equal to \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A})\). The dice are independent.

Dependent events \(\color{#325D88}{C}\) is “the total is six”

Five outcomes remain, and one has a three on the first die, so \(P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{C}) = \tfrac{1}{5}\). The total tells you something about the first die.

Here \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\) is “the first die is a three”. Reversing the conditioning gives a different question, which Bayes’ theorem answers.

Conditioning Narrows the Sample Space

Eight in ten office managers would buy the software (\(\color{#325D88}{A}\)), and four in ten of those would also upgrade (\(\color{#F47C3C}{B}\)). Of the rest, one in ten would. Given \(\color{#F47C3C}{B}\), how likely is \(\color{#325D88}{A}\)?

Conditioning on \(\color{#F47C3C}{B}\) excludes the other 66%, so \(P(\color{#325D88}{A} \mid \color{#F47C3C}{B}) = P(\color{#325D88}{A} \cap \color{#F47C3C}{B})/P(\color{#F47C3C}{B})\).

Reading a Two-Way Table

Choose an event and a condition. The table marks the cells used in the numerator and denominator of the probability.

ctCols = ["Accountancy", "Economics", "Finance", "Business Info"]
ctRows = ["Male", "Female"]
ctN = [[330, 360, 90, 120], [120, 390, 60, 30]]
ctTotal = 1500
// The cells an event covers, keyed "row,col".
ctCells = ev => new Set(ctRows.includes(ev)
  ? ctCols.map((_, j) => `${ctRows.indexOf(ev)},${j}`)
  : ctRows.map((_, i) => `${i},${ctCols.indexOf(ev)}`))
ctCount = s => [...s].reduce((t, k) => {
  const [i, j] = k.split(",").map(Number);
  return t + ctN[i][j];
}, 0)
viewof ctA = Inputs.radio([...ctRows, ...ctCols],
  {value: "Economics", label: "Probability of"})
viewof ctB = Inputs.radio(["Nothing", ...ctRows, ...ctCols],
  {value: "Female", label: "Given"})
ctView = {
  const A = ctCells(ctA);
  const B = ctB === "Nothing" ? null : ctCells(ctB);
  const top = B ? new Set([...A].filter(k => B.has(k))) : A;
  const num = ctCount(top), den = B ? ctCount(B) : ctTotal;
  // Navy marks what you divide by; orange, the deck's "the part you want",
  // marks what goes on top. A cell can be both.
  const cls = (i, j) => {
    const k = `${i},${j}`;
    return [top.has(k) ? "ct-top" : "", (!B || B.has(k)) ? "ct-den" : ""].join(" ");
  };
  const rowSum = i => ctN[i].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const colSum = j => ctN[0][j] + ctN[1][j];
  const f3 = v => v.toFixed(3);
  const lhs = B ? `P(${ctA} | ${ctB})` : `P(${ctA})`;
  let verdict;
  if (!B) {
    verdict = html`Nothing is given, so you divide by all ${ctTotal} students.`;
  } else if (num === 0) {
    verdict = html`No student is both. The two events are <b>mutually exclusive</b>, so knowing one rules the other out.`;
  } else if (ctA === ctB) {
    verdict = html`Told it happened, it is certain.`;
  } else {
    const pA = ctCount(A) / ctTotal;
    const same = Math.abs(num / den - pA) < 0.0005;
    verdict = html`Without the condition, P(${ctA}) = ${ctCount(A)} / ${ctTotal} = ${f3(pA)}.
      ${same ? html`The same, so the two are <b>independent</b>.`
             : html`Knowing ${ctB} changes it, so the two are <b>not independent</b>.`}`;
  }
  return html`<div class="ct-wrap">
    <table class="ct-table">
      <thead><tr><th></th>${ctCols.map(c => html`<th>${c}</th>`)}<th class="ct-sum">Total</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        ${ctRows.map((r, i) => html`<tr><th>${r}</th>
          ${ctCols.map((_, j) => html`<td class=${cls(i, j)}>${ctN[i][j]}</td>`)}
          <td class="ct-sum">${rowSum(i)}</td></tr>`)}
        <tr class="ct-sum"><th>Total</th>${ctCols.map((_, j) => html`<td>${colSum(j)}</td>`)}<td>${ctTotal}</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="ct-eq">${lhs} = <span class="ct-num">${num}</span> / <span class="ct-dnm">${den}</span> = ${f3(num / den)}</div>
    <div class="quiz-fb">${verdict}</div>
  </div>`;
}

Independence of taxi breakdowns

Each taxi has an independent chance of breaking down, so multiply the individual probabilities to find the probability of a particular combination. Set the rates, then put the two old taxis in the same garage.

viewof txOld = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: 0.10, step: 0.01, format: v => v.toFixed(2), label: "Old taxi breaks down"})
viewof txNew = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: 0.05, step: 0.01, format: v => v.toFixed(2), label: "New taxi breaks down"})
viewof txShared = Inputs.toggle({label: "Old pair share a garage", value: false})
txDays = 1000000
txSim = {
  let all4 = 0, newOnly = 0;
  for (let d = 0; d < txDays; d++) {
    const o1 = Math.random() < txOld;
    const o2 = txShared ? o1 : Math.random() < txOld;
    const n1 = Math.random() < txNew, n2 = Math.random() < txNew;
    if (o1 && o2 && n1 && n2) all4++;
    if (!o1 && !o2 && n1 && n2) newOnly++;
  }
  return {all4: all4 / txDays, newOnly: newOnly / txDays};
}
txRule = ({all4: txOld * txOld * txNew * txNew,
           newOnly: (1 - txOld) * (1 - txOld) * txNew * txNew})
{
  const g = v => v.toFixed(6);   // one width for every cell, 0.000025 needs six
  const o = txOld.toFixed(2), n = txNew.toFixed(2), q = (1 - txOld).toFixed(2);
  const verdict = txShared
    ? html`The second old taxi now has the same breakdown outcome as the first. The simulated probability is about <b>${(1 / txOld).toFixed(0)} times</b> the product of the four individual probabilities. Multiplying those probabilities requires <b>independence</b>, which is why the worksheet asks you to state this assumption.`
    : html`The product and simulation agree within sampling variation over a million days. The breakdowns are independent, so their individual probabilities can be multiplied.`;
  return html`<div class="ct-wrap">
    <table class="ct-table">
      <thead><tr><th></th><th>Product rule</th><th>${d3.format(",")(txDays)} days simulated</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><th>All four break down</th><td>${o} × ${o} × ${n} × ${n} = ${g(txRule.all4)}</td><td class=${txShared ? "ct-top" : ""}>${g(txSim.all4)}</td></tr>
        <tr><th>Only the new ones break down</th><td>${q} × ${q} × ${n} × ${n} = ${g(txRule.newOnly)}</td><td class=${txShared ? "ct-top" : ""}>${g(txSim.newOnly)}</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="quiz-fb ${txShared ? "quiz-no" : "quiz-ok"}">${verdict}</div>
  </div>`;
}

The Law of Total Probability

Partition \(\Omega\) into events that do not overlap and cover the sample space. Calculate the probability of \(\color{#93C54B}{A}\) within each part, then add the results.

\[P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \sum_{i} P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B_i})\, P(\color{#325D88}{B_i})\]

Supplier 1 Half the parts, two per hundred faulty

\[0.50 \times 0.02 = 0.010\]

Supplier 2 Three parts in ten, four per hundred faulty

\[0.30 \times 0.04 = 0.012\]

Supplier 3 One part in five, seven per hundred faulty

\[0.20 \times 0.07 = 0.014\]

Adding the three routes gives \(P(\text{faulty}) = 0.036\). To find the probability that a faulty part came from a particular supplier, use Bayes’ theorem.

Librarian or Farmer?

Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or in the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.

The answer depends on the base rate, which the description does not give. The next slide includes the number of people in each occupation.

Twenty Farmers for Every Librarian

The base rate gives the relative frequency of each occupation before considering Steve’s description. The description is four times as likely for a librarian, while farmers are twenty times as common. Steve is therefore five times as likely to be a farmer.

Bayes’ theorem

Changing the prior probability

Effect of the prior probability

The evidence stays the same as you change the prior. 1/21 corresponds to one librarian for every twenty farmers; at 0.50 you get 0.80. The base rate supplies the relative frequency of the two occupations.

Monty Hall Problem

A car sits behind one of three doors and a goat behind each of the others. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 on a goat and offers you the swap. Do you take it?

Discrete Distributions

Random variables, binomial and Poisson

Random Variables

A random variable assigns a number to each outcome in the sample space. We can then calculate with these numerical outcomes.

\[X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \qquad\qquad P(X = x)\]

Discrete Values you can list

Roll two dice and let \(\color{#93C54B}{X}\) be the total. It is the number already written in every cell of the board.

3 + 42 + 56 + 1

Six of the thirty-six cells carry a 7, so

\(P(\color{#93C54B}{X} = 7) = \tfrac{6}{36}\)

Continuous Values filling a range

Wait at a bus stop and let \(\color{#325D88}{X}\) be the minutes until the next arrival. It can be 3, or 3.1, or 3.0004.

3.03.13.0004

Each individual value has probability zero. Calculate the probability of an interval:

\(P(2 \le \color{#325D88}{X} \le 4)\)

The calculation depends on the type of variable. A discrete variable gives every value its own probability and you add them up. A continuous one spreads probability along a line and you measure the area under a curve. The binomial and the Poisson ahead are discrete, the exponential and the normal are continuous.

A Distribution Is a Function

For each value of \(X\), \(P\) gives the probability of that value. Writing this function gives the distribution without having to repeat the counting.

\[\sum_{k} P(X = k) = 1 \qquad\qquad \int p(x)\,dx = 1\]

Flip a coin four times \(\Omega\) has sixteen outcomes, \(\color{#93C54B}{X}\) counts the heads

Using a distribution Probabilities, modelling and interval calculations

The function \(P(\color{#93C54B}{X})\) gives the probabilities without requiring a separate count for each value.

A distribution models the process. Data can be used to test the model and estimate its parameters.

Add the bars over a range, or measure the area under the curve, and you have \(P(a \le \color{#93C54B}{X} \le b)\).

Two examples are the binomial and normal distributions. Heads in \(n\) flips is the binomial, and a height or a measurement error is the normal, written \(\color{#93C54B}{X} \sim \text{Binomial}\) and \(\color{#325D88}{X} \sim \text{Normal}\).

Passing within three attempts

A student passes each attempt with probability \(p\) and gets three tries. Among those who passed, on which attempt did they do it?

viewof atP = Inputs.range([0.1, 0.95], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Pass rate per attempt"})
atRaw = [1, 2, 3].map(x => Math.pow(1 - atP, x - 1) * atP)   // pass first at x
atC = d3.sum(atRaw)                                          // = 1 - (1 - p)^3
atBars = [1, 2, 3].flatMap((x, i) => [
  {x, kind: "before", v: atRaw[i]},
  {x, kind: "after", v: atRaw[i] / atC}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 250, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 54, marginTop: 22,
  style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
  // The x ticks are the key: grey is every student, green only those who passed.
  fx: {label: null, padding: 0.25, tickFormat: d => `Passed on attempt ${d}`, axis: "bottom", tickPadding: 32},
  x: {label: null, domain: ["before", "after"], padding: 0.1, tickSize: 0,
      tickFormat: d => d === "before" ? "Everyone" : "Given passed"},
  y: {domain: [0, 1], grid: true, label: "probability", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(atBars, {fx: "x", x: "kind", y: "v",
      fill: d => d.kind === "after" ? PPAL.olive : PPAL.dim}),
    Plot.text(atBars, {fx: "x", x: "kind", y: "v", dy: -10,
      text: d => d.v.toFixed(3), fill: PPAL.soft, fontSize: 14}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
html`<div class="ojs-eq at-eq">${atRaw.map(v => v.toFixed(3)).join(" + ")} = <span class="rate">${atC.toFixed(3)}</span> &nbsp;→&nbsp; divide each by <span class="rate">${atC.toFixed(3)}</span> &nbsp;→&nbsp; <span class="hit">sum = 1</span></div>
<div class="quiz-fb">The grey bars sum to less than one. The remaining probability is <b>${(1 - atC).toFixed(3)}</b>, the students who fail all three attempts and are not in the group you sampled from. Dividing by ${atC.toFixed(3)} is <b>conditioning on "passed"</b>, and gives green bars whose probabilities sum to one.</div>`

Which Seller Do You Trust?

Three sellers offer the same item at the same price on a marketplace. Choose a seller using their customer reviews.

How would you weigh the greater confidence from more reviews against a lower percentage of positive reviews?

Laplace’s Rule of Succession

Laplace’s 1774 rule adds one hypothetical positive review and one negative review to the observed reviews. This gives \((k+1)/(n+2)\) in place of \(k/n\).

What assumptions does this rule use? How would changing them affect your choice?

Where the Binomial Comes From

Every review is an independent draw at one constant unknown rate \(S\). Start with a proposed value of \(S\) and calculate what it predicts.

What If the Rate Were Different?

Choose a value of \(S\). The top plot shows the resulting distribution; the bottom plot shows the probability of the observed count as a function of \(S\).

viewof s = Inputs.range([0.50, 1.00], {value: 0.95, step: 0.01, label: "True success rate S"})
n = 50
k = 48

// The deck's palette, so the plots match the hand-drawn stages either side.
PAL = ({olive: "#93C54B", brick: "#B94A48", navy: "#325D88",
        orange: "#F47C3C", soft: "#6E7681", dim: "#B0B7C0"})

// Binomial pmf by recurrence: P(0) = (1-p)^n, then
// P(j) = P(j-1) * (n-j+1)/j * p/(1-p). No factorial is ever formed, so
// nothing overflows — the same route stage-kit.html uses.
pmf = function (p) {
  const q = 1 - p;
  if (q <= 0) return Array.from({length: n + 1}, (_, i) => (i === n ? 1 : 0));
  let v = Math.pow(q, n);
  const out = [v];
  for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) { v = v * ((n - j + 1) / j) * (p / q); out.push(v); }
  return out;
}

pk = pmf(s)
value = pk[k]
lik = d3.range(0, 1.0005, 0.004).map(sv => ({s: sv, p: pmf(sv)[k]}))

PSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
Plot.plot({
  // marginTop 16, not 4: at 4 the 30% tick label has no room above the top

  y: {domain: [0, 0.30], ticks: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], grid: true,

Plot.plot({

The Binomial in Standard Notation

We now write the binomial distribution in standard notation. The rate we have been calling \(S\) is written \(\color{#F47C3C}{p}\); its complement is \(\color{#B94A48}{q} = 1 - \color{#F47C3C}{p}\).

\[P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \binom{n}{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\; \color{#F47C3C}{p}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}\; \color{#B94A48}{q}^{\,\color{#B94A48}{n-k}} \qquad X \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n, \color{#F47C3C}{p})\]

One review is a Bernoulli trial, a single attempt with two outcomes, scored \(1\) for good and \(0\) for bad.

\[P(B_i = 1) = \color{#F47C3C}{p}, \quad P(B_i = 0) = \color{#B94A48}{q}, \quad \operatorname{E}[B_i] = \color{#F47C3C}{p}, \quad \operatorname{Var}(B_i) = \color{#F47C3C}{p}\color{#B94A48}{q}\]

\[X \;=\; B_1 + B_2 + \cdots + B_n, \qquad B_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\color{#F47C3C}{p})\]

Each of seller B’s fifty reviews was one \(B_i\). Their sum has a binomial distribution, which records the total count.

The Rare Event Limit of a Binomial Distribution

Keep the average \(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} = n\,\color{#F47C3C}{p}\) fixed and increase \(n\). Each trial gets rarer, but you expect the same number of events.

viewof nTrials = Inputs.range([10, 400], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Trials n"})
// Floor of 10, not 5: lam runs to 8, and n < lam would ask for p > 1, which
// the recurrence below happily turns into a 1971% gap. NB a comment must NOT
// be the first line of an {ojs} cell: it shadows the '//|' directive and
// Quarto then emits the whole slide as plain source, with no runtime and no
// error anywhere.
viewof lam = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 3, step: 0.5, label: "Mean λ = np"})
PPAL = ({olive: "#93C54B", brick: "#B94A48", navy: "#325D88",
         orange: "#F47C3C", soft: "#6E7681", dim: "#B0B7C0"})

pp = lam / nTrials                       // the success rate, shrinking as nTrials grows
KMAX = Math.max(12, Math.ceil(lam + 4 * Math.sqrt(lam)))
ks = d3.range(0, KMAX + 1)

// Binomial(nTrials, pp) by the same recurrence used everywhere else in this deck
binom = {
  const q = 1 - pp;
  if (q <= 0) return ks.map(k => (k === nTrials ? 1 : 0));
  let v = Math.pow(q, nTrials);
  const out = [v];
  const top = Math.min(nTrials, KMAX);   // KMAX <= 20; no point walking to 20,000
  for (let j = 1; j <= top; j++) { v = v * ((nTrials - j + 1) / j) * (pp / q); out.push(v); }
  return ks.map(k => (k <= nTrials ? out[k] : 0));
}

// Poisson(lam): P(0) = e^-lam, then P(k) = P(k-1) * lam / k
pois = {
  const out = []; let v = Math.exp(-lam);
  for (let k = 0; k <= KMAX; k++) { out.push(v); v = v * lam / (k + 1); }
  return out;
}

gap = d3.max(ks, k => Math.abs(binom[k] - pois[k]))
YMAX = Math.max(d3.max(binom), d3.max(pois)) * 1.18
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 205, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 26, marginTop: 16,
  style: {fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
          color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [-0.6, KMAX + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YMAX], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ks, {x: d => d, y2: d => binom[d], strokeWidth: 9,
      stroke: PPAL.dim, clip: true}),
    // "step" is Plot's midpoint step (d3.curveStep); "step-mid" is not a
    // curve name and throws, taking the whole plot cell with it.
    Plot.line(ks, {x: d => d, y: d => pois[d], stroke: PPAL.brick,
      strokeWidth: 2, curve: "step", clip: true}),
    Plot.dot(ks, {x: d => d, y: d => pois[d], fill: PPAL.brick, r: 3.2,
      clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
html`<div class="ojs-eq">Binomial(${nTrials}, <span class="rate">${pp.toFixed(4)}</span>) &nbsp;→&nbsp; <span class="miss">Poisson(${lam.toFixed(1)})</span> &nbsp;·&nbsp; gap <b>${(100*gap).toFixed(2)}%</b></div>`

As \(n\) increases, the shape depends on the product of \(n\) and \(\color{#F47C3C}{p}\) rather than their separate values. The Poisson therefore has one parameter.

The Poisson in Standard Notation

Put \(\color{#F47C3C}{p} = \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}/n\) into the binomial and let \(n\) tend to infinity.

\[P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \binom{n}{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\big(\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{n-\color{#93C54B}{k}}\]

↓ Group the factors by whether they still mention \(n\)

\[=\;\frac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}}{\color{#93C54B}{k}!}\;\cdot\;\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-\color{#93C54B}{k}+1)}{n^{\color{#93C54B}{k}}}\;\cdot\;\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{n}\;\cdot\;\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{-\color{#93C54B}{k}}\]

↓ As \(n \to \infty\) those three go to \(1\), to \(e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}\), and to \(1\)

\[P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \frac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}}{\color{#93C54B}{k}!} \qquad X \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda})\]

The middle factor gives the exponential term, since \((1-\lambda/n)^{n}\) is the definition of \(e^{-\lambda}\). The result has one parameter, and \(\operatorname{E}[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}\).

Check the Approximation

Exact vs approximate

An audit covers 10,000 transactions, with a rate of three mistakes per 10,000. Calculate the probability of four or more mistakes using the binomial and Poisson distributions.

Both read 0.3527681, so they agree to every digit R prints. Now set n <- 20; p <- 0.15 (still \(np = 3\)) and compare the results. The approximation is less accurate when \(n\) is smaller and \(p\) is larger.

Continuous Distributions

Exponential, uniform, normal, chi-square and t distributions

Time Between Poisson Events

The \(\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}\) bar, no arrivals, links the count to the waiting time.

viewof lamE = Inputs.range([0.5, 4], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "Rate λ per minute"})
viewof winT = Inputs.range([0.1, 2.5], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Window t minutes"})
muE = lamE * winT                     // arrivals expected in the window
KMAXE = Math.max(8, Math.ceil(muE + 4 * Math.sqrt(muE)))
ksE = d3.range(0, KMAXE + 1)

// Poisson(muE) by the deck's usual recurrence: P(0) = e^-mu, P(k) = P(k-1) mu/k
poisE = {
  const out = []; let v = Math.exp(-muE);
  for (let k = 0; k <= KMAXE; k++) { out.push(v); v = v * muE / (k + 1); }
  return out;
}

// The whole point of the slide: the k = 0 bar IS the exponential's survival
// curve. P(no arrival in [0, t]) = e^(-lambda t) = P(wait > t).
p0E = Math.exp(-muE)
TE = 3                                // minutes on the bottom axis
densE = t => lamE * Math.exp(-lamE * t)
gridE = d3.range(0, 241).map(i => TE * i / 240)
tailE = d3.range(0, 161).map(i => winT + (TE - winT) * i / 160)
YPOIS = d3.max(poisE) * 1.18
YDENS = lamE * 1.12
ESTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 136, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
  style: ESTYLE,
  x: {domain: [-0.6, KMAXE + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YPOIS], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k arrivals in t)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ksE, {x: d => d, y2: d => poisE[d], strokeWidth: 7,
      stroke: d => (d === 0 ? PPAL.olive : PPAL.dim), clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
html`<div class="ojs-eq">P(<span class="hit">0 arrivals</span> in ${winT.toFixed(2)} min) &nbsp;=&nbsp; <b>${p0E.toFixed(4)}</b> &nbsp;=&nbsp; P(<span class="hit">wait &gt; ${winT.toFixed(2)}</span>) &nbsp;·&nbsp; <span class="rate">λ = ${lamE.toFixed(1)}</span></div>`
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 136, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
  style: ESTYLE,
  x: {domain: [0, TE], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YDENS], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".1f")(d),
      label: "density of the wait", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    // This olive area is the same number as the olive bar above it.
    Plot.areaY(tailE, {x: t => t, y: densE, fill: PPAL.olive,
      fillOpacity: 0.3, clip: true}),
    Plot.line(gridE, {x: t => t, y: densE, stroke: PPAL.brick,
      strokeWidth: 2.5, clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([winT], {stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})

The Exponential in Standard Notation

Waiting longer than \(t\) means no events in \([0, t]\): the Poisson at \(\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}\).

\[P(T > t) \;=\; P\big(N(t) = \color{#93C54B}{0}\big), \qquad N(t) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t)\]

↓ Put \(\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}\) into the Poisson formula

\[=\;\frac{(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t)^{\color{#93C54B}{0}}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}}{\color{#93C54B}{0}!} \;=\; e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}\]

↓ That is the survival curve, so the density is the slope of \(1 - e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}\)

\[f(t) \;=\; \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t} \qquad T \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda})\]

Both distributions use the same rate \(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}\). \(\operatorname{E}[T] = 1/\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}\) is the average gap between arrivals.

The uniform distribution

When every value between \(a\) and \(b\) is equally likely, the density is flat. A probability is then a length times the height, and the height is whatever makes the whole area one.

viewof unIn = Inputs.form({
  a: Inputs.range([-5, -1], {value: -2, step: 1, label: "Lower end a"}),
  b: Inputs.range([1, 6], {value: 4, step: 1, label: "Upper end b"}),
  c: Inputs.range([-5, 6], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "Cut-off c"})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="un-dials">${Object.values(ins)}</div>`})
unA = unIn.a
unB = unIn.b
unC = unIn.c
unW = unB - unA
unH = 1 / unW
unLo = Math.min(Math.max(unC, unA), unB)            // the part of [c, b] inside [a, b]
unP = (unB - unLo) / unW
unMu = (unA + unB) / 2
unVar = unW * unW / 12
unSd = Math.sqrt(unVar)
unFrac = (n, d) => d === 1 ? `${n}` : `${n}/${d}`
// A block, not `unGcd = (x, y) => ... unGcd(...)`: an OJS cell that names
// itself is a circular definition.
unGcd = { const g = (x, y) => y ? g(y, x % y) : Math.abs(x); return g; }
unPf = unFrac((unB - unLo) / unGcd(unB - unLo, unW), unW / unGcd(unB - unLo, unW))
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 181, marginLeft: 72, marginBottom: 30, marginTop: 15,
  style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
  x: {domain: [-6, 7], label: null, ticks: d3.range(-6, 8), tickSize: 4},
  // a <= -1 and b >= 1 keep the width at 2 or more, so the height never
  // passes 0.5 and one fixed axis shows it rise as the interval narrows.
  y: {domain: [0, 0.75], grid: true, ticks: [0, 0.25, 0.5], tickFormat: d => d, label: "f(x)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 58},
  marks: [
    // the shaded probability, olive like every "the part you want" on these slides
    Plot.rectY([0], {x1: unLo, x2: unB, y: unH, fill: PPAL.olive, fillOpacity: 0.35}),
    Plot.line([[-6, 0], [unA, 0], [unA, unH], [unB, unH], [unB, 0], [7, 0]],
      {stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([unMu - unSd, unMu + unSd], {y1: 0, y2: unH + 0.12, stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
    Plot.ruleX([unMu], {y1: 0, y2: unH + 0.12, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.text(["μ"], {x: unMu, y: unH + 0.12, dy: -10, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.brick, fontSize: 18, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.ruleX([unC], {stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeDasharray: "2 3"}),
    // the y axis drawn as a line, so the ticks hang off something
    Plot.ruleX([-6], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
html`<div class="ojs-eq cr-eqs un-eqs">
  <span>f(x)</span><span>= 1 / (b − a) = 1 / (${unB} − (${unA})) = 1/${unW}</span>
  <span>P(X ≥ ${unC})</span><span>= length × height = ${unB - unLo} × 1/${unW} = <span class="hit">${unPf}</span></span>
  <span>E[X]</span><span>= (a + b) / 2 = <span class="miss">${unMu}</span></span>
  <span>Var(X)</span><span>= (b − a)² / 12 = ${unW * unW} / 12 = <span class="rate">${+unVar.toFixed(4)}</span></span>
</div>`

The Limit of a Binomial Distribution for Large n

Keep \(\color{#F47C3C}{p}\) fixed and increase \(n\). The bars approach a bell shape.

viewof nBig = Inputs.range([5, 200], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Trials n"})
viewof pBig = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {value: 0.35, step: 0.05, label: "Success rate p"})
muB = nBig * pBig
sdB = Math.sqrt(nBig * pBig * (1 - pBig))
kLo = Math.max(0, Math.floor(muB - 4 * sdB))
kHi = Math.min(nBig, Math.ceil(muB + 4 * sdB))
ksB = d3.range(kLo, kHi + 1)

// Binomial(nBig, pBig) by the deck's usual recurrence, walked only as far as
// the plot shows: P(0) = (1-p)^n, P(j) = P(j-1) (n-j+1)/j p/(1-p).
binomB = {
  const q = 1 - pBig;
  let v = Math.pow(q, nBig);
  const out = [v];
  for (let j = 1; j <= kHi; j++) { v = v * ((nBig - j + 1) / j) * (pBig / q); out.push(v); }
  return out;
}

// De Moivre's curve: N(np, np(1-p)), read as a density at each whole k.
normB = x => Math.exp(-((x - muB) ** 2) / (2 * sdB * sdB)) / (sdB * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))
gapB = d3.max(ksB, k => Math.abs(binomB[k] - normB(k)))
YMAXB = d3.max(ksB, k => Math.max(binomB[k], normB(k))) * 1.18
BWB = Math.max(1.5, Math.min(9, 880 / (kHi - kLo + 1) - 1))
gridB = d3.range(0, 241).map(i => kLo + (kHi - kLo) * i / 240)
BSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 205, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 26, marginTop: 16,
  style: BSTYLE,
  x: {domain: [kLo - 0.6, kHi + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YMAXB], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ksB, {x: d => d, y2: d => binomB[d], strokeWidth: BWB,
      stroke: PPAL.dim, clip: true}),
    Plot.line(gridB, {x: d => d, y: normB, stroke: PPAL.navy,
      strokeWidth: 2.5, clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
html`<div class="ojs-eq">Binomial(${nBig}, <span class="rate">${pBig.toFixed(2)}</span>) &nbsp;→&nbsp; <span class="miss">N(${muB.toFixed(1)}, ${(sdB*sdB).toFixed(1)})</span> &nbsp;·&nbsp; gap <b>${(100*gapB).toFixed(2)}%</b></div>`

The binomial has two limiting distributions. Rare events with \(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} = n\color{#F47C3C}{p}\) held fixed give the Poisson, plenty of events with \(\color{#F47C3C}{p}\) held fixed give the normal.

The Galton Board

In Galton’s 1889 machine, each peg sends a ball left or right. The number of right turns follows a binomial distribution.

The Normal Distribution

\(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}\) slides the curve, \(\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}\) stretches it, and its area is always 1.

\[f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}\sqrt{2\pi}}\; e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}}\right)^{2}}\]

nfDens = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - nfMu) / nfSig) ** 2) / (nfSig * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))
nfGrid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => -4 + 8 * i / 400)
nfPeak = nfDens(nfMu)
nfArrowY = Math.min(nfPeak + 0.1, 1.1)
// the reference N(0, 1), and the stretch within one σ of the centre
nfStd = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)
nfBand = d3.range(0, 121).map(i => nfMu - nfSig + 2 * nfSig * i / 120)
NFSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
            color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
viewof nf = Inputs.form({
  sig: Inputs.range([0.4, 2], {value: 0.84, step: 0.01, label: htl.html`Spread <b style="color:${PPAL.orange}">σ</b>`}),
  mu:  Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.34, step: 0.01, label: htl.html`Centre <b style="color:${PPAL.brick}">μ</b>`})
}, {template: ins => htl.html`<div class="nf-dials">${Object.values(ins)}</div>`})
nfSig = nf.sig
nfMu = nf.mu
// Three readings. Only the first moves: the area and the ±σ share are the
// same for every normal, which is the point of showing them beside it.
html`<div class="nf-card">
  <div><span>Peak height</span><b>${nfPeak.toFixed(3)}</b></div>
  <div><span>Area under the curve</span><b>1</b></div>
  <div><span>Within μ ± σ</span><b class="nf-band">68.3%</b></div>
</div>`
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 330, marginLeft: 56, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 20, marginRight: 10,
  style: NFSTYLE,
  x: {domain: [-4, 4], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  // up to 1.1: room for σ = 0.4, whose peak is 0.997, and the arrows over it
  y: {domain: [0, 1.1], grid: true, ticks: [0, 0.5, 1], label: "f(x)",
      labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 46},
  marks: [
    // the reference: N(0, 1), dashed, behind everything
    Plot.line(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfStd, stroke: PPAL.dim, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 5"}),
    Plot.areaY(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, fill: PPAL.navy, fillOpacity: 0.08}),
    // within one σ of the centre: always 68.3% of the area
    Plot.areaY(nfBand, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, fill: PPAL.orange, fillOpacity: 0.18}),
    Plot.line(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    // the peak, read across to the axis: 1/(σ√2π), never 1 unless σ ≈ 0.4
    Plot.ruleY([nfPeak], {x1: -4, x2: nfMu, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeDasharray: "2 4", strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
    Plot.dot([nfMu], {x: d => d, y: nfPeak, r: 4.5, fill: PPAL.navy}),
    Plot.text([nfPeak], {x: -4, y: d => d, dx: 4, dy: -9, textAnchor: "start",
      text: d => d.toFixed(3), fill: PPAL.navy, fontSize: 14, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text(["N(0, 1)"], {x: 2.6, y: nfStd(2.6) + 0.07, text: d => d,
      fill: PPAL.soft, fontSize: 14}),
    Plot.ruleX([nfMu - nfSig, nfMu + nfSig], {y1: 0, y2: nfArrowY + 0.05,
      stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([nfMu], {y1: 0, y2: nfArrowY + 0.05, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.arrow([-1, 1], {x1: nfMu, x2: d => nfMu + d * nfSig, y1: nfArrowY, y2: nfArrowY,
      stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 2.5, headLength: 10, inset: 4}),
    Plot.text([-1, 1], {x: d => nfMu + d * nfSig / 2, y: nfArrowY, dy: -12, text: () => "σ",
      fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text([nfMu], {x: d => d, y: nfArrowY + 0.05, dy: -12, text: () => "μ",
      fill: PPAL.brick, fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700}),
    // in the left half of the band, clear of the μ line at every σ
    Plot.text([nfMu - nfSig / 2], {x: d => d, y: nfPeak * 0.3, text: () => "68.3%",
      fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})

Terms in the normal density

Each term controls part of the curve. The \(e\) and the square make the bell, \(\sigma\) sets its width, \(\mu\) moves it, and the constant in front keeps the area at 1.

Where the \(e\) in the Normal Comes From

Suppose errors in two directions are independent and no direction is preferred. These conditions determine the bell shape.

Where the \(\pi\) in the Normal Comes From

Call \(C\) the area under the bell \(e^{-x^2}\). Form a surface from the product of two such curves, then calculate its volume in two ways.

Areas Under the Normal

A probability is an area under the bell. Standardising only relabels the axis.

naErf = x => { const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * x);
  return 1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x); }
Phi = z => 0.5 * (1 + Math.sign(z) * naErf(Math.abs(z) / Math.SQRT2))
naKinds = ["X < a", "X > a", "a < X < b", "X < a or X > b"]
// Numbers rather than sliders: any normal at all, typed in. The defaults are
// the last part of the worksheet's N(100, 64) question, as a starting point.
viewof naIn = Inputs.form({
  mu: Inputs.number({value: 100, step: 1, label: "Mean μ"}),
  sd: Inputs.number({value: 8, step: 0.5, min: 0.1, label: "SD σ"}),
  a:  Inputs.number({value: 90, step: 0.5, label: "a"}),
  b:  Inputs.number({value: 100, step: 0.5, label: "b"})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="na-dials">${Object.values(ins)}</div>`})
viewof naKind = Inputs.radio(naKinds, {value: "a < X < b", label: "Probability"})
{
  const mu = naIn.mu, sd = Math.max(naIn.sd || 1, 0.1);
  const a = Math.min(naIn.a, naIn.b), b = Math.max(naIn.a, naIn.b);   // typed either way round
  const one = naKind === "X < a" || naKind === "X > a";
  const z = x => (x - mu) / sd, za = z(a), zb = z(b);
  const f = v => +v.toFixed(4), fz = v => (Math.abs(v) < 5e-4 ? 0 : +v.toFixed(3));
  const pa = Phi(za), pb = Phi(zb);
  const [p, xl, zl, route] = {
    "X < a":          [pa, `P(X < ${a})`, `P(Z < ${fz(za)})`, `${f(pa)}`],
    "X > a":          [1 - pa, `P(X > ${a})`, `P(Z > ${fz(za)})`, `1 − P(Z < ${fz(za)}) = 1 − ${f(pa)}`],
    "a < X < b":      [pb - pa, `P(${a} < X < ${b})`, `P(${fz(za)} < Z < ${fz(zb)})`, `P(Z < ${fz(zb)}) − P(Z < ${fz(za)}) = ${f(pb)} − ${f(pa)}`],
    "X < a or X > b": [1 - (pb - pa), `P(X < ${a} or X > ${b})`, `P(Z < ${fz(za)} or Z > ${fz(zb)})`, `1 − (${f(pb)} − ${f(pa)})`]
  }[naKind];
  const lo = mu - 4 * sd, hi = mu + 4 * sd;
  const pieces = {"X < a": [[lo, a]], "X > a": [[a, hi]], "a < X < b": [[a, b]],
                  "X < a or X > b": [[lo, a], [b, hi]]}[naKind];
  const dens = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * z(x) ** 2) / (sd * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  const grid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => lo + (hi - lo) * i / 400);
  const tk = v => +v.toFixed(2);
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 950, height: 236, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 46, marginTop: 22,
    style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
    // Ticks at mu + k sigma, so the z under each is a whole number: two rulers, one area.
    x: {domain: [lo, hi], label: null, ticks: d3.range(-3, 4).map(k => mu + k * sd), tickSize: 4,
        tickFormat: d => `${tk(d)}\nz = ${Math.round((d - mu) / sd)}`},
    y: {domain: [0, 1.15 * dens(mu)], axis: null},
    marks: [
      ...pieces.map(([u, v]) => Plot.areaY(grid.filter(x => x >= u && x <= v), {x: d => d, y: dens,
        fill: PPAL.olive, fillOpacity: 0.35})),
      Plot.line(grid, {x: d => d, y: dens, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.ruleX([mu], {y1: 0, y2: dens(mu), stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleX(one ? [a] : [a, b], {stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeDasharray: "2 3", clip: true}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
    ]
  });
  // One [left, right] pair per line of working; flattened, since each is two grid cells.
  const rows = [
    [xl, `= ${zl}, with z = (x − ${mu}) / ${sd}`],
    ["", `= ${route}`],
    ["", html`= <span class="hit">${p.toFixed(4)}</span>`]
  ];
  return html`${plot}<div class="ojs-eq cr-eqs na-eqs">
    ${rows.flatMap(([l, r]) => [html`<span>${l}</span>`, html`<span>${r}</span>`])}
  </div>`;
}

Finding a Cut-Off

To find a critical value, specify the central probability and divide the remaining probability equally between the tails. Use the table to find the corresponding boundary.

viewof ncC = Inputs.range([0.5, 0.98], {value: 0.8, step: 0.01, format: v => v.toFixed(2), label: "Central area"})
ncMu = 4
ncSd = 1.5
ncB = { let lo = -8, hi = 8; const t = (1 + ncC) / 2;
        for (let i = 0; i < 80; i++) { const m = (lo + hi) / 2; Phi(m) < t ? lo = m : hi = m; }
        return (lo + hi) / 2; }
ncA = ncSd * ncB
{
  const lo = ncMu - 4 * ncSd, hi = ncMu + 4 * ncSd, tail = (1 - ncC) / 2;
  const dens = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - ncMu) / ncSd) ** 2) / (ncSd * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  const grid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => lo + (hi - lo) * i / 400);
  const top = dens(ncMu);
  const lo2 = Math.floor(ncB * 100) / 100, hi2 = lo2 + 0.01;   // the two table entries either side
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 950, height: 260, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 4,
    style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
    x: {domain: [lo, hi], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, top * 1.12], axis: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(grid.filter(x => Math.abs(x - ncMu) <= ncA), {x: d => d, y: dens, fill: PPAL.olive, fillOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.line(grid, {x: d => d, y: dens, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.ruleX([ncMu], {y1: 0, y2: top, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleX([ncMu - ncA, ncMu + ncA], {y1: 0, y2: top * 0.75, stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.text([ncMu - ncA, ncMu + ncA], {x: d => d, y: top * 0.75, dy: -10, fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700,
        text: (d, i) => i ? "4 + a" : "4 − a"}),
      Plot.text([ncMu], {x: d => d, y: top * 0.35, text: () => `${(100 * ncC).toFixed(0)}%`, fill: "#3E3F3A", fontSize: 18, fontWeight: 700}),
      Plot.text([lo + 1.2 * ncSd, hi - 1.2 * ncSd], {x: d => d, y: top * 0.18, text: () => `${(100 * tail).toFixed(1)}%`, fill: PPAL.soft, fontSize: 16}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
    ]
  });
  return html`${plot}<div class="ojs-eq cr-eqs na-eqs nc-eqs">
    <span>P(Z &lt; b)</span><span>= (1 + ${ncC.toFixed(2)}) / 2 = ${((1 + ncC) / 2).toFixed(3)}, with b = a / ${ncSd}</span>
    <span>b</span><span>= <span class="rate">${ncB.toFixed(4)}</span> &nbsp;<span class="na-note">Table: P(Z &lt; ${lo2.toFixed(2)}) = ${Phi(lo2).toFixed(4)}, P(Z &lt; ${hi2.toFixed(2)}) = ${Phi(hi2).toFixed(4)}</span></span>
    <span>a</span><span>= ${ncSd} × ${ncB.toFixed(4)} = <span class="hit">${ncA.toFixed(2)}</span></span>
  </div>`;
}

The Box Plot on a Normal Curve

A box plot summarises five values without assuming a distribution. On a normal curve, their positions show how the \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) rule relates to the distribution.

\(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) sit at \(\mp 0.6745\sigma\), so the fences fall at \(\mp 2.698\sigma\) and only \(0.7\%\) of a normal lies beyond them. In a normal sample of a thousand, the rule flags about seven points.

Functions of a Random Variable

For \(\color{#93C54B}{Y} = g(X)\), use the CDF to find which values of \(X\) satisfy \(\color{#93C54B}{Y} \le y\).

\[F_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; P(a X + b \le y) \;=\; P\big(X \le \tfrac{y-b}{a}\big)\]

↓ The right-hand side is just \(X\)’s own CDF, read at a shifted point

\[F_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; F_X\big(\tfrac{y-b}{a}\big)\]

↓ Differentiate in \(y\); the chain rule brings down the \(1/a\)

\[f_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{|a|}\, f_X\big(\tfrac{y-b}{a}\big) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \color{#93C54B}{Y} \sim \operatorname{N}\big(a\mu + b,\; a^{2}\sigma^{2}\big)\]

Standardising is this with \(a = 1/\sigma\) and \(b = -\mu/\sigma\), which is why one table serves every normal. A non-linear \(g\) leaves the family, so \(X \sim \operatorname{N}(0,1)\) makes \(\color{#93C54B}{Y} = X^{2}\) chi-squared.

The Chi-Square Distribution

Square \(k\) independent standard normals and add them up. The total is never negative, and it describes the distribution of scaled sample variances, since \((n-1)s^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\).

The Student’s \(t\) Distribution

Replacing the unknown \(\sigma\) with the sample standard deviation \(S\) gives a distribution with heavier tails. Formally \(T = Z/\sqrt{V/k}\) with \(V \sim \chi^2_k\), which is why the chi-square came first.

Relationships Among Probability Distributions

Each distribution is one step from another: a sum, a limit, a square or a ratio.

Expectation and Limit Theorems

Mean, variance, Chebyshev, LLN and CLT

Expected Value, Variance and Standard Deviation

Comparing delivery times

The two firms have the same four possible delivery times, with different probabilities. The red line is the mean and the orange lines sit one standard deviation either side.

viewof crFirm = Inputs.radio(["Firm A", "Firm B"], {value: "Firm A", label: "Show the working for"})
crX = [0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]
crP = ({"Firm A": [0.6, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2], "Firm B": [0.1, 0.7, 0.15, 0.05]})
crMom = p => {
  const mu = d3.sum(crX, (x, i) => x * p[i]);
  const ex2 = d3.sum(crX, (x, i) => x * x * p[i]);
  return {mu, ex2, v: ex2 - mu * mu, sd: Math.sqrt(ex2 - mu * mu)};
}
crPlot = firm => {
  const p = crP[firm], m = crMom(p);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 460, height: 190, marginLeft: 48, marginBottom: 30, marginTop: 26,
    style: ({fontSize: "14px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
    x: {domain: [0, 2.5], label: null, ticks: crX, tickSize: 4, tickFormat: d => `${d} h`},
    y: {domain: [0, 0.8], grid: true, ticks: [0, 0.4, 0.8], label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX(crX, {x: d => d, y2: (d, i) => p[i], strokeWidth: 16,
        stroke: firm === crFirm ? PPAL.navy : PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.ruleX([m.mu - m.sd, m.mu + m.sd], {stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleX([m.mu], {stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.text([firm], {frameAnchor: "top-right", dy: -18, text: d => d,
        fill: firm === crFirm ? PPAL.navy : PPAL.soft, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
    ]
  });
}
{
  const p = crP[crFirm], m = crMom(p);
  const f = v => +v.toFixed(4);
  const terms = crX.map((x, i) => `${x}²×${p[i]}`).join(" + ");
  return html`<div class="cr-row">${crPlot("Firm A")}${crPlot("Firm B")}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq cr-eqs">
    <span>E[X]</span><span>= ${crX.map((x, i) => `${x}×${p[i]}`).join(" + ")} = <span class="miss">${f(m.mu)}</span></span>
    <span>E[X²]</span><span>= ${terms} = ${f(m.ex2)}</span>
    <span>Var(X)</span><span>= E[X²] − μ² = ${f(m.ex2)} − ${f(m.mu)}² = <span class="rate">${f(m.v)}</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">Firm A has a lower mean delivery time (0.95 h against 1.075 h). Firm B has a lower variance (0.107 against 0.373). The choice depends on the relative costs of late and slower deliveries.</div>`;
}

Chebyshev’s inequality

Chebyshev

Chebyshev’s inequality states that at least \(1 - 1/k^2\) of any distribution lies within \(k\) standard deviations. It does not require normality or symmetry.

The bound is loose because it applies without specifying the distribution’s shape. Swap rexp(n, 1)^2 for rnorm(n) and the gap widens further: for a normal, \(k = 2\) captures 95%, not the 75% Chebyshev guarantees.

The Law of Large Numbers, Intuitively

The Idea Behind the Central Limit Theorem

Simulating sums of dice

Throw \(\color{#F47C3C}{n}\) of them and add them up, 2,500 times.

The Two Limit Theorems, Formally

Take \(\color{#F47C3C}{n}\) independent draws from the same distribution (i.i.d.), each with mean \(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and average them.

\[\bar X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \;=\; \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} X_i\]

Law of large numbers Convergence of the sample mean

\[\bar X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \;\longrightarrow\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \qquad \text{as } \color{#F47C3C}{n} \to \infty\]

For any margin \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(P(|\bar X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}| \ge \varepsilon) \to 0\). With enough draws the mean is as close to \(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}\) as you like.

Central limit theorem Distribution of the sample mean

\[\bar X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \;\approx\; N\Big(\color{#B94A48}{\mu},\, \frac{\sigma^2}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}}\Big) \qquad \text{SD} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\color{#F47C3C}{n}}}\]

Whatever the shape of the \(X_i\), for large \(\color{#F47C3C}{n}\) the mean is close to normal, and its spread shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{\color{#F47C3C}{n}}\).

The LLN is the running mean settling on \(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}\); the CLT describes the approximately normal distribution of the sample mean, narrowing as \(\color{#F47C3C}{n}\) grows.

Choosing a display for the data

Tick the display that suits each set of data. The reasoning appears underneath.
