  const NAVY = "#325D88";
  const wrap = inner =>
    `<svg width="42" height="26" viewBox="0 0 42 26" aria-hidden="true">${inner}</svg>`;
  // Bars on a 40-wide strip sitting on a baseline at y = 22. A histogram's
  // bars touch and a bar chart's do not, which is the one difference a
  // student is meant to read off these thumbnails.
  const bars = (hs, pitch, w) => hs.map((h, i) =>
    `<rect x="${2 + i * pitch}" y="${22 - h}" width="${w}" height="${h}" fill="${NAVY}"/>`
  ).join("");
  const line = (x1, y1, x2, y2) =>
    `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>`;
  return ({
    "Bar or pie": wrap(bars([16, 9, 13, 6], 10, 7)),
    "Histogram": wrap(bars([5, 12, 18, 11, 5], 8, 8)),
    "Scatter plot": wrap([[5,20],[11,16],[16,18],[21,13],[26,11],[32,8],[38,5]]
      .map(([x, y]) => `<circle cx="${x}" cy="${y}" r="2.1" fill="${NAVY}"/>`).join("")),
    "Time series": wrap(
      `<polyline points="3,20 10,12 17,16 24,7 31,11 39,4" fill="none"
         stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/>`),
    "Box plot": wrap(line(3, 13, 12, 13) + line(28, 13, 39, 13) +
      `<rect x="12" y="7" width="16" height="12" fill="none" stroke="${NAVY}" stroke-width="1.6"/>` +
      line(21, 7, 21, 19))
  });
}
viewof ccI = Inputs.radio([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {value: 1, label: "Question"})
ccPrompt = html`<div class="quiz-q">${ccQ[ccI - 1].q}</div>`
viewof ccPick = {
  ccI;   // naming it here rebuilds the input when the question changes, which
         // is the only way to clear the previous answer's ticks
  // html([...]) rather than html`...`: the sketch is a string of markup and
  // the tagged form would escape it into visible angle brackets.
  // radio, not checkbox: every question has exactly one right display, so
  // letting the room tick three of them only invites a wrong kind of answer.
  return Inputs.radio(ccOpts, {
    label: "Suitable display",
    format: v => html([`<span class="quiz-opt">${ccIcon[v]}<span>${v}</span></span>`])
  });
}
ccFeedback = {
  const want = ccQ[ccI - 1].a;
  if (!ccPick) return html`<div class="quiz-fb quiz-idle">Pick a display to see the reasoning.</div>`;
  const ok = ccPick === want;
  // A wrong pick names the job the chosen chart does and points back at the
  // data. It does NOT name the answer: handing it over ends the thinking, and
  // the radio is still there to try again with.
  const text = ok
    ? html`<b>Yes.</b> ${ccQ[ccI - 1].why}`
    : html`<b>Not quite.</b> ${ccJob[ccPick]}. ${ccQ[ccI - 1].hint}`;
  // The plot always shows the display that was PICKED, not the right one —
  // on a wrong answer it is the thing they asked for, which is an argument
  // rather than a giveaway.
  return html`<div class="quiz-answer">
    <div class="quiz-fb ${ok ? "quiz-ok" : "quiz-no"}">${text}</div>
    <figure class="quiz-plot">
      <figcaption>${ccPick}</figcaption>
      ${ccDemo[ccPick]()}
    </figure>
  </div>`;
}

Thirteen Salaries at a Small Firm

The Same Thirteen Salaries, in R

Descriptive statistics

Each summary from the previous slide can be calculated with one line of R.

Change the last salary to 96 and run it again. The mode and median stay the same in this example. The mean and standard deviation change because they depend on the size of the last salary.

Sampling a Distribution Randomly

In survey sampling, we draw a small random sample from a larger population. Distinguish the population quantities from the corresponding sample quantities.

Population Large, size \(\color{#325D88}{N}\)

\[\begin{gathered} \{x_1, \dots, x_{\color{#325D88}{N}}\} \\[4pt] \color{#B94A48}{\mu} = \frac{1}{\color{#325D88}{N}} \sum_{j=1}^{\color{#325D88}{N}} x_j \qquad \color{#F47C3C}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{\color{#325D88}{N}} \sum_{j=1}^{\color{#325D88}{N}} (x_j - \color{#B94A48}{\mu})^2 \end{gathered}\]

These are fixed population quantities that we want to estimate. Equivalently \(\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{N}\sum x_j^2 - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2\).

Sample Small, size \(\color{#F47C3C}{n}\)

\[\begin{gathered} \{X_1, \dots, X_{\color{#F47C3C}{n}}\} \\[4pt] \color{#F47C3C}{\bar X} = \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} X_i \qquad \color{#F47C3C}{\widehat{\sigma}^{2}} = \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\color{#F47C3C}{n}} (X_i - \color{#F47C3C}{\bar X})^2 \end{gathered}\]

These quantities can be calculated from the sample and vary from one sample to another. R’s var() gives \(s^2\), which divides by \(n - 1\) instead and removes a small bias.

There are \(\binom{N}{n}\) possible samples of size \(n\). Simple random sampling (without replacement) makes each one equally likely.

Three Properties of the Sample Mean

The sample mean \(\bar X\) changes from sample to sample, so it is itself a random variable; the number you compute from your data is its value, \(\bar x\). The following properties describe its use as an estimator of \(\mu\).

Unbiased

\(\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu\)

Its expected value equals the population mean.

Efficient

\(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \dfrac{N - n}{N - 1}\)

The smallest variance of any unbiased weighted average.

Consistent

\(\bar X \to \mu \;\text{ as }\; n \to N\)

The estimate approaches \(\mu\) as \(n\) increases; at \(n = N\) it equals \(\mu\).

Drawn without replacement, the \(X_i\) are not independent, and that shrinks the variance by \(\frac{N - n}{N - 1}\), the finite population correction. When \(N \gg n\) it is close to 1, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \approx \sigma^2/n\), the formula the intervals use.

Proving Unbiasedness

Draw \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) without replacement from \(N\) units \(x_1, \dots, x_N\). Each unit is equally likely to be the \(i\)-th draw, so \(P(X_i = x_j) = 1/N\).

\[\textstyle \operatorname{E}[X_i] \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} x_j\, P(X_i = x_j) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} x_j \cdot \frac{1}{N} \;=\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu}\]

↓ The same sum with \((x_j - \mu)^2\) gives \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2\). Now average the \(n\) draws

\[\textstyle \operatorname{E}[\bar X] \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{E}[X_i] \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\, n\mu \;=\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{unbiased}}\]

↓ Why the second step needs no independence

\[\textstyle \operatorname{E}[X + Y] = \sum (x + y)\, P(x, y) = \sum x\, P(x) + \sum y\, P(y) = \operatorname{E}[X] + \operatorname{E}[Y]\]

Only each variable’s own probabilities appear, never \(P(x, y) = P(x)\,P(y)\), so \(\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu\) with or without replacement.

Proving the Variance and Consistency

With replacement the draws are independent: \(P(X_2 = x_l \mid X_1 = x_k) = 1/N\). Without, it is \(1/(N-1)\) or 0, so let \(c = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\).

\[\textstyle 0 \;=\; \operatorname{Var}(X_1 + \dots + X_N) \;=\; N\sigma^2 + N(N-1)\,c \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; c = -\frac{\sigma^2}{N-1}\]

↓ At \(n = N\) the total is fixed, which determines the covariance. The same expansion for \(n\) draws

\[\textstyle \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\Big[\, n\sigma^2 - n(n-1)\frac{\sigma^2}{N-1} \Big] \;=\; \color{#325D88}{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1}}\]

↓ Chebyshev, \(P(|Y - \operatorname{E}[Y]| \ge \varepsilon) \le \operatorname{Var}(Y)/\varepsilon^2\), with \(Y = \bar X\)

\[\textstyle P\big(|\bar X - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\big) \;\le\; \frac{\sigma^2}{n\,\varepsilon^2} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1} \;\to\; 0 \;\text{ as }\; n \to N \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{consistent}}\]

The factor is 1 with replacement (\(c = 0\)) or at \(n = 1\); close to 1 when \(N \gg n\).

The Sample Variance

The hat marks an estimate: \(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}\) is the population formula run on the sample, so it is random. Is its expected value equal to \(\sigma^2\)?

\[\textstyle \widehat{\sigma}^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 \;-\; \bar X^2\]

↓ Take expectations with \(\operatorname{E}[Y^2] = \operatorname{Var}(Y) + \operatorname{E}[Y]^2\), for \(Y = X_i\) and for \(Y = \bar X\)

\[\textstyle \operatorname{E}[\widehat{\sigma}^{2}] \;=\; (\sigma^2 + \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2) \;-\; \Big(\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1} + \color{#B94A48}{\mu}^2\Big) \;=\; \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{N(n-1)}{n(N-1)}\]

↓ Biased, a little below \(\sigma^2\). Rescale; as \(N \to \infty\) this is \(s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (X_i - \bar X)^2\)

\[\textstyle \operatorname{E}\Big[\frac{n(N-1)}{N(n-1)}\, \widehat{\sigma}^{2}\Big] \;=\; \color{#325D88}{\sigma^2} \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{unbiased}}\]

So the unknown \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\) can be estimated from the data by \(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}\, \frac{N-n}{N(n-1)}\).

Normal Approximation to the Distribution of \(\bar X\)

By the CLT, for large \(n\) the sample mean is close to normal, with spread the standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) (taking \(N \gg n\)).

The approximation Centre \(\mu\), spread \(\sigma/\sqrt n\)

\[\bar X \approx N\Big(\color{#B94A48}{\mu}, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\Big) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0, 1) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; P\Big(\frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le a\Big) \to \Phi(a)\]

How close is \(\bar X\) to \(\mu\)? Divide every side by \(\sigma/\sqrt n\)

\[P(|\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}| < \varepsilon) = P\Big({-\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}} < Z < \frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}\Big) = \Phi\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}\Big) - \Phi\Big({-\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt n}{\sigma}}\Big)\]

A Confidence Interval for \(\mu\)

A \((1 - \alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is a random interval, centred at \(\bar X\), that contains \(\mu\) with probability \(1 - \alpha\). The derivation is below.

\[\textstyle P\big(-q \le \bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \le q\big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha\]

↓ Divide by the standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt n\); the cut-off becomes \(z_{\alpha/2}\), with \(\Phi(z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 - \alpha/2\)

\[\textstyle P\Big(-z_{\alpha/2} \le \frac{\bar X - \color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le z_{\alpha/2}\Big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha\]

↓ Multiply through by \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) and rearrange around \(\mu\)

\[\textstyle P\Big(\bar X - z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \;\le\; \color{#B94A48}{\mu} \;\le\; \bar X + z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Big) \;=\; 1 - \alpha\]

So \(\bar X \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n\) is the interval; for 95%, \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\).

Calculating a confidence interval

Example: \(\sigma = 15\) is known, and a sample of \(n = 25\) gives \(\bar x = 103.2\). Build the 95% interval.

Before sampling, \(\bar X \pm 5.88\) is random and contains \(\mu\) with probability 0.95. Once we observe \(\bar x = 103.2\), \((97.32, 109.08)\) is fixed: it contains \(\mu\) or it does not. The 95% describes the method across repeated samples.

From the sampling distribution to an interval

To see why it works, use \(\mu = 100\) for illustration. In practice, \(\mu\) is unknown.

\(\bar x \pm 5.88\) contains \(\mu\) exactly when \(\bar x\) falls within 5.88 of \(\mu\), which happens 95% of the time.

Interpreting a confidence interval

Tempting

“My interval contains \(\mu\) with 95% probability.”

Correct

“95% of intervals built this way contain \(\mu\).”

Simulate the Sample Mean and Its Interval

viewof clIn = Inputs.form({
  n: Inputs.range([2, 200], {value: 10, step: 1, label: html`Sample size <i style="text-transform: none">n</i>`}),
  conf: Inputs.range([0.8, 0.99], {value: 0.95, step: 0.01, label: "Confidence"}),
  rule: Inputs.radio(["Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n", "Unknown σ: x̄ ± z·s/√n", "Unknown σ: x̄ ± t·s/√n"], {value: "Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n", label: "Interval"}),
  again: Inputs.button("New samples")
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="cl-dials">${ins.n}${ins.conf}${ins.again}</div><div class="cl-dials cl-rule">${ins.rule}</div>`})
clLgam = x => { const c = [76.18009172947146, -86.50532032941677, 24.01409824083091,
    -1.231739572450155, 0.1208650973866179e-2, -0.5395239384953e-5];
  let y = x, t = x + 5.5, s = 1.000000000190015; t -= (x + 0.5) * Math.log(t);
  for (const ci of c) s += ci / ++y;
  return -t + Math.log(2.5066282746310005 * s / x); }
clBetacf = (a, b, x) => { let c = 1, d = 1 / (1 - (a + b) * x / (a + 1)), h = d;
  for (let m = 1; m < 200; m++) { const m2 = 2 * m;
    let aa = m * (b - m) * x / ((a + m2 - 1) * (a + m2));
    d = 1 / (1 + aa * d); c = 1 + aa / c; h *= d * c;
    aa = -(a + m) * (a + b + m) * x / ((a + m2) * (a + m2 + 1));
    d = 1 / (1 + aa * d); c = 1 + aa / c; const del = d * c; h *= del;
    if (Math.abs(del - 1) < 1e-12) break; }
  return h; }
clIbeta = (a, b, x) => { if (x <= 0) return 0; if (x >= 1) return 1;
  const bt = Math.exp(clLgam(a + b) - clLgam(a) - clLgam(b) + a * Math.log(x) + b * Math.log(1 - x));
  return x < (a + 1) / (a + b + 2) ? bt * clBetacf(a, b, x) / a : 1 - bt * clBetacf(b, a, 1 - x) / b; }
clTcdf = (t, df) => { const p = 0.5 * clIbeta(df / 2, 0.5, df / (df + t * t)); return t > 0 ? 1 - p : p; }
clInv = cdf => p => { let lo = 0, hi = 1000;
  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) { const m = (lo + hi) / 2; cdf(m) < p ? lo = m : hi = m; }
  return (lo + hi) / 2; }
clMu = 100
clSd = 15
clReps = 2000
// Seeded from the button count, so moving the confidence slider or the
// interval rule re-draws the SAME samples: only the intervals change.
clSim = {
  const n = clIn.n, rnd = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(((clIn.again + 1) * 0.6180339887) % 1))(clMu, clSd);
  const xbar = [], s = [], row = new Float64Array(n);
  for (let r = 0; r < clReps; r++) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) row[i] = rnd();
    xbar.push(d3.mean(row)); s.push(d3.deviation(row));
  }
  return {n, xbar, s};
}
{
  const {n, xbar, s} = clSim, p = (1 + clIn.conf) / 2, rn = Math.sqrt(n);
  const crit = clIn.rule === "Unknown σ: x̄ ± t·s/√n" ? clInv(t => clTcdf(t, n - 1))(p) : clInv(Phi)(p);
  const half = xbar.map((_, r) => crit * (clIn.rule === "Known σ: x̄ ± z·σ/√n" ? clSd : s[r]) / rn);
  const hit = xbar.map((x, r) => Math.abs(x - clMu) <= half[r]);
  const cover = d3.mean(hit, h => +h);
  const style = ({fontSize: "14px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"});
  const T = d3.range(clMu - 25, clMu + 25.01, 1);
  const dist = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 245, marginLeft: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [clMu - 25, clMu + 25], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {axis: null, insetTop: 18},   // headroom so the peak clears the title
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(xbar, Plot.binX({y: "proportion"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: T, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5})),
      Plot.ruleX([clMu], {stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.text(["Means of 2,000 samples from N(100, 15²)"], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16})
    ]
  });
  const idx = d3.range(50);
  const ints = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 245, marginLeft: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [clMu - 30, clMu + 30], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [-1, 50], axis: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(idx, {y: i => i, x1: i => xbar[i] - half[i], x2: i => xbar[i] + half[i], clip: true,
        stroke: i => hit[i] ? "#9FB6CC" : PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(idx, {y: i => i, x: i => xbar[i], r: 1.8, fill: i => hit[i] ? PPAL.navy : PPAL.brick}),
      Plot.text(["The first 50 intervals"], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16}),
      Plot.ruleX([clMu], {stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"})
    ]
  });
  const f = (v, k = 2) => v.toFixed(k);
  // The verdict reads the run, so it changes as the controls do.
  const pct = v => `<b>${f(100 * v, 1)}%</b>`, target = `${Math.round(100 * clIn.conf)}%`;
  const verdict = (n, c) => clIn.rule === "Unknown σ: x̄ ± z·s/√n" && c < clIn.conf - 0.02
    ? `With s in place of σ and n = ${n}, the z cut-off is too narrow: only ${pct(c)} of the intervals contain μ, not ${target}. <b>Switch to t</b> to account for uncertainty in the estimate of σ.`
    : `The mean X̄ centres on μ (<b>unbiased</b>) and its variance σ²/n shrinks as n grows (<b>consistent</b>). ${pct(c)} of the intervals contain μ, close to the specified ${target} confidence level.`;
  return html`<div class="cr-row">${dist}${ints}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq cl-stats">
    <span>Mean of <span class="cl-bar">X</span> ≈ ${f(d3.mean(xbar))} <span class="na-note">(μ = ${clMu})</span></span>
    <span>Var(<span class="cl-bar">X</span>) ≈ <span class="cl-navy">${f(d3.variance(xbar))}</span> <span class="na-note">(σ²/n = ${f(clSd ** 2 / n)})</span></span>
    <span>Coverage = <span class="${Math.abs(cover - clIn.conf) < 0.02 ? "hit" : "miss"}">${f(100 * cover, 1)}%</span> <span class="na-note">(cut-off ${f(crit, 3)})</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${verdict(n, cover)}</div>`;
}

Forty Punts

An NFL punter has historically averaged 41 yards a punt, with a standard deviation of 8 yards. What is the probability that their next 40 punts average at least 45 yards?

The average of 40 punts Its centre and its standard error

\[\begin{gathered} \bar X_{40} = \frac{1}{40}\sum_{i=1}^{40} X_i \\ \operatorname{E}[\bar X_{40}] = \color{#B94A48}{41} \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\bar X_{40}) = \frac{8}{\sqrt{40}} = 1.26 \end{gathered}\]

By the CLT Standardise, then read the table

\[\begin{aligned} P(\bar X_{40} \ge 45) &= P\Big(\frac{\bar X_{40} - 41}{8/\sqrt{40}} \ge \frac{45 - 41}{8/\sqrt{40}}\Big) \\ &= P(Z \ge 3.16) = 1 - \Phi(3.16) \\ &= 7.8 \times 10^{-4} \end{aligned}\]

About 1 in 1,300. Forty punts averaging 45 yards would be 3.16 standard errors above the punter’s history.

Example after Dr. John Quintanilla, as told by Steve Brunton.

Hypothesis Testing

Tests for one and two population means

Testing the effect of a marketing campaign

A website averaged \(\mu = 10{,}372\) visits a day. After a marketing campaign, 30 days give a sample mean \(\bar x = 10{,}628\), with sample SD 402. Did the campaign work?

Two explanations Null and alternative hypotheses

A. \(H_0\): the mean has not changed, \(\mu = 10{,}372\); the rise is chance.

B. \(H_1\): the mean has increased, \(\mu > 10{,}372\); the rise is too large to be random.

Procedure Calculating the test statistic and p-value

I. Assume \(H_0\) is true: the average is still \(10{,}372\).

II. Count the standard errors between \(\bar x\) and \(\mu_0\):

\[z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt n} = \frac{10{,}628 - 10{,}372}{402/\sqrt{30}} \approx 3.49\]

III. The p-value: \(p = P(Z \ge 3.49) = 0.0002\), the chance of a \(z\) this large if \(H_0\) were true.

IV. Choose \(\alpha = 0.05\) beforehand: reject \(H_0\) when \(z \ge z_{0.05} = 1.645\), the same as \(p < 0.05\). Here \(3.49 \ge 1.645\): reject \(H_0\).

402 is a sample SD, so strictly this is the \(t\) case of the next slides: \(t = 3.49\) on 29 df gives \(p \approx 0.0008\). The conclusion is unchanged.

Four Steps of a Test

A test compares the sample mean \(\bar x\) with a hypothesised population mean \(\mu_0\), allowing for sampling variation. Use the following four steps.

Hypotheses

\(H_0\!: \mu = \mu_0\)

State the null hypothesis and the alternative \(H_1\).

Statistic

\(z = \dfrac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt n}\)

How many standard errors \(\bar x\) lies from \(\mu_0\).

Critical Value

\(z > z_\alpha\)

Reject \(H_0\) if the statistic lands past the cut-off.

P-Value

\(p < \alpha\)

Or reject if the tail area beyond it is below \(\alpha\).

The last two always agree: the statistic is past the cut-off exactly when the area beyond it is below \(\alpha\).

The z and t Test Statistics

Both count standard errors between \(\bar x\) and \(\mu_0\); the choice of table depends on whether \(\sigma\) is known.

\[\textstyle Z = \frac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\color{#325D88}{\sigma} / \sqrt n} \sim N(0, 1) \;\; \color{#6E7681}{\sigma \text{ known}} \qquad\quad T = \frac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\color{#B94A48}{S} / \sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1} \;\; \color{#6E7681}{\sigma \text{ unknown}}\]

↓ The alternative \(H_1\) decides which tail or tails to use

Alternative \(H_1\) Reject \(H_0\) if P-value
\(\mu > \mu_0\) \(z > z_\alpha\) \(p = P(Z > z)\)
\(\mu < \mu_0\) \(z < -z_\alpha\) \(p = P(Z < z)\)
\(\mu \neq \mu_0\) \(\lvert z \rvert > z_{\alpha/2}\) \(p = 2P(Z > \lvert z \rvert)\)

With \(t\), use \(t_\alpha\) on \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom. Its critical values are larger in magnitude, so the same statistic can reject \(H_0\) in a \(z\) test and fail to reject it in a \(t\) test.

Comparing the sample with the null hypothesis

Test \(H_0\!: \mu = \mu_0\) against \(H_1\!: \mu > \mu_0\). Our sample gave \(z = 2.0\). Is that surprising if \(H_0\) is true?

Tail probability If \(H_0\) were true, a \(z\) at least as large as ours would come up less than 5% of the time. That is rare enough to reject \(H_0\).

Repeated experiments If \(H_0\) is true and I repeat the experiment, chance alone produces a result at least this extreme only \(p\)% of the time: here about 2.3%.

Rejection Region and P-Value

// Defaults are Exercise 1 of the beamer Seminar 5: z = 2.5, right-tailed, 5%.
viewof rjIn = Inputs.form({
  test: Inputs.radio(["Normal z", "Student's t"], {value: "Normal z", label: "Test"}),
  df: Inputs.range([1, 60], {value: 24, step: 1, label: "Degrees of freedom"}),
  tail: Inputs.radio(["Left", "Right", "Two-tailed"], {value: "Right", label: "Tail"}),
  alpha: Inputs.range([0.01, 0.1], {value: 0.05, step: 0.005, label: html`Significance <i style="text-transform: none">α</i>`}),
  stat: Inputs.range([-4, 4], {value: 2.5, step: 0.01, label: "Observed statistic"})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="rj-dials">${ins.test}${ins.df}${ins.tail}</div><div class="rj-dials">${ins.alpha}${ins.stat}</div>`})
rjTdens = (x, df) => Math.exp(clLgam((df + 1) / 2) - clLgam(df / 2) - 0.5 * Math.log(df * Math.PI)
  - (df + 1) / 2 * Math.log(1 + x * x / df))
rjDens = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)
// Cut-off c (positive), p-value and decision for one test; cdf is its CDF.
rjRule = (cdf, tail, a, s) => {
  const c = clInv(cdf)(1 - (tail === "Two-tailed" ? a / 2 : a));
  const p = tail === "Right" ? 1 - cdf(s) : tail === "Left" ? cdf(s) : 2 * (1 - cdf(Math.abs(s)));
  const rej = tail === "Right" ? s > c : tail === "Left" ? s < -c : Math.abs(s) > c;
  return {c, p, rej};
}
{
  const isT = rjIn.test === "Student's t", df = rjIn.df, {tail, alpha, stat} = rjIn;
  const cdf = isT ? (x => clTcdf(x, df)) : Phi, dens = isT ? (x => rjTdens(x, df)) : rjDens;
  const {c, p, rej} = rjRule(cdf, tail, alpha, stat);
  const sym = isT ? "t" : "z", lo = -4.5, hi = 4.5, s = Math.abs(stat);
  const grid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => lo + (hi - lo) * i / 400);
  const reg = {Right: [[c, hi]], Left: [[lo, -c]], "Two-tailed": [[lo, -c], [c, hi]]}[tail];
  const pv = {Right: [[stat, hi]], Left: [[lo, stat]], "Two-tailed": [[lo, -s], [s, hi]]}[tail];
  const cuts = reg.map(([u, v]) => u === lo ? v : u);
  const top = rjDens(0), f = (v, k = 3) => v.toFixed(k).replace("-", "−");   // a true minus sign
  const area = (pieces, fill, op) => pieces.map(([u, v]) => Plot.areaY(grid.filter(x => x >= u && x <= v),
    {x: d => d, y: dens, fill, fillOpacity: op}));
  const halo = {stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6};
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 920, height: 270, marginLeft: 20, marginRight: 20, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 34,
    style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
    x: {domain: [lo, hi], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, top * 1.02], axis: null},
    marks: [
      ...area(reg, PPAL.brick, 0.3),
      ...area(pv, PPAL.orange, 0.45),
      Plot.line(grid, {x: d => d, y: dens, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.ruleX(cuts, {y1: 0, y2: top * 0.6, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.text(cuts, {x: d => d, y: top * 0.6, dy: -10, text: d => f(d), fill: PPAL.brick, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700, ...halo}),
      Plot.ruleX([stat], {y1: 0, y2: top * 0.88, stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.text([stat], {x: d => d, y: top * 0.88, dy: -10, text: d => `${sym} = ${f(d, 2)}`, fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700, ...halo}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.text([isT ? `Null distribution: t with ${df} degrees of freedom` : "Null distribution: N(0, 1)"],
        {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -28, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16, ...halo})
    ]
  });
  // Exercise 5: on t, say what z would have decided with the same statistic.
  const z = rjRule(Phi, tail, alpha, stat);
  const cs = v => tail === "Two-tailed" ? `±${f(v)}` : f(tail === "Left" ? -v : v);
  const alt = isT && z.rej !== rej
    ? ` With z the cut-off would be ${cs(z.c)} and we would ${z.rej ? "reject" : "fail to reject"}: the heavier t tails give a larger critical value.` : "";
  const msg = `The statistic ${sym} = ${f(stat, 2)} is ${rej ? "inside" : "outside"} the rejection region (cut-off ${cs(c)}), and its p-value ${f(p, 4)} is ${p < alpha ? "below" : "above"} α = ${+alpha.toFixed(3)}: <b>${rej ? "reject" : "fail to reject"} H₀</b>.${alt}`;
  return html`${plot}
  <div class="ojs-eq cl-stats">
    <span>Critical value = <span class="miss">${cs(c)}</span></span>
    <span>P-value = <span class="rate">${f(p, 4)}</span></span>
    <span>Decision: ${rej ? "Reject H₀" : "Fail to reject H₀"}</span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${msg}</div>`;
}

Four Outcomes of a Test

Combining the two test decisions with whether \(H_0\) is true gives four possible outcomes. Two are correct decisions and two are errors.

Actual truth
H₀ is trueH₀ is false
DecisionReject H₀ Type I error
probability α (5%)		 Correct
probability 1 − β, the power
Fail to reject H₀ Correct
probability 1 − α		 Type II error
probability β

\(\alpha\) is the significance level, chosen before looking at the data; \(1 - \beta\) is the power, the probability of detecting a real change. The next slide shows how \(n\) and \(\alpha\) trade them off.

Type I and Type II Errors

pwMu0 = 1300
pwSd = 720
viewof pwIn = Inputs.form({
  mu: Inputs.range([1300, 1900], {value: 1600, step: 10, label: html`True mean <i style="text-transform: none">μ</i>`}),
  n: Inputs.range([9, 144], {value: 36, step: 1, label: html`Sample size <i style="text-transform: none">n</i>`}),
  alpha: Inputs.range([0.01, 0.1], {value: 0.05, step: 0.005, label: html`Significance <i style="text-transform: none">α</i>`})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="rj-dials">${Object.values(ins)}</div>`})
{
  const {mu, n, alpha} = pwIn, se = pwSd / Math.sqrt(n);
  const c = pwMu0 + clInv(Phi)(1 - alpha) * se;          // reject H0 when the sample mean exceeds c
  const beta = Phi((c - mu) / se), power = 1 - beta;
  const lo = pwMu0 - 4 * se, hi = Math.max(mu, pwMu0) + 4 * se;
  const grid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => lo + (hi - lo) * i / 400);
  const dn = m => x => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m) / se) ** 2) / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  const d0 = dn(pwMu0), d1 = dn(mu), top = d0(pwMu0), same = mu === pwMu0;
  const halo = {stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6};
  const f = (v, k = 1) => v.toFixed(k), pc = v => `${f(100 * v)}%`;
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 1000, height: 300, marginLeft: 20, marginRight: 20, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 40,
    style: ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"}),
    x: {domain: [lo, hi], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, top * 1.15], axis: null, insetTop: 12},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(grid.filter(x => x <= c), {x: d => d, y: d1, fill: PPAL.orange, fillOpacity: same ? 0 : 0.4}),
      Plot.areaY(grid.filter(x => x >= c), {x: d => d, y: d0, fill: PPAL.brick, fillOpacity: 0.45}),
      Plot.line(grid, {x: d => d, y: d1, stroke: PPAL.olive, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.line(grid, {x: d => d, y: d0, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeDasharray: same ? "6 4" : null}),
      Plot.ruleX([c], {y1: 0, y2: top * 1.05, stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.text([c], {x: d => d, y: top * 0.55, dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", text: d => `Cut-off ${f(d)}`, fill: "#3E3F3A", fontSize: 15, ...halo}),
      Plot.text([pwMu0], {x: d => d, y: top, dy: -10, text: d => `H₀: μ = ${d}`, fill: PPAL.navy, fontSize: 15, fontWeight: 700, ...halo}),
      ...(same ? [] : [Plot.text([mu], {x: d => d, y: top, dy: -10, text: d => `True μ = ${d}`, fill: PPAL.olive, fontSize: 15, fontWeight: 700, ...halo})]),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.text([`Sample means under H₀ and under the true mean, σ/√n = ${f(se)}`],
        {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -28, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16, ...halo})
    ]
  });
  const msg = same
    ? `The true mean is μ₀, so H₀ holds and the only possible mistake is a <b>Type I error</b>: rejecting it anyway, ${pc(alpha)} of the time.`
    : `If the true mean is ${mu}, a sample of ${n} days lands past the cut-off with probability <b>${pc(power)}</b>, the power. It misses ${pc(beta)} of the time, a <b>Type II error</b>. A larger n shrinks β; a smaller α cuts false alarms but widens β.`;
  return html`${plot}
  <div class="ojs-eq cl-stats">
    <span>Type I: <span class="miss">α = ${pc(alpha)}</span></span>
    <span>Type II: <span class="rate">${same ? "None, H₀ is true" : `β = ${pc(beta)}`}</span></span>
    <span>Power = <span class="hit">${same ? "n/a" : pc(power)}</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${msg}</div>`;
}

Three Ways to Compare Two Means

Each test divides the gap between two sample means by its standard error. How the data were collected decides which standard error to use.

Pooled t

\(t = \dfrac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\)

Independent samples, normal, equal variances. Compare with \(t_{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\).

Large samples

\(z = \dfrac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}\)

Independent samples, unequal variances, large \(n\). Compare with \(N(0, 1)\).

Paired t

\(t = \dfrac{\bar d}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}\)

The same units measured twice. Test the differences \(d\) against \(t_{n - 1}\).

The next slide builds the pooled test and its interval; the two after it show why paired data must not be treated as independent.

Pooling the Two Variances

Both samples estimate one shared variance \(\sigma^2\), so we pool them, weighting each by its degrees of freedom.

\[\textstyle s_p^2 \;=\; \frac{(n_1 - 1)\,s_1^2 \;+\; (n_2 - 1)\,s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]

↓ Put \(s_p^2\) in place of \(\sigma^2\) in the standard error of \(\bar x_1 - \bar x_2\)

\[\textstyle T \;=\; \frac{(\bar X_1 - \bar X_2) \,-\, (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{S_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \;\sim\; \color{#325D88}{t_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\]

↓ Rearrange the test inequality to obtain a confidence interval

\[\textstyle \mu_1 - \mu_2 \;\in\; (\bar x_1 - \bar x_2) \;\pm\; \color{#B94A48}{t_{\alpha/2,\; n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\, \sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\]

Repeated measurements on the same firms

Variation in cost of equity between firms can obscure the change between periods. Calculating each firm’s difference removes its initial level, allowing each firm to act as its own control.

Paired and independent samples tests

viewof plIn = Inputs.form({
  mode: Inputs.radio(["Paired", "Independent"], {value: "Paired", label: "Treat the data as"}),
  alpha: Inputs.radio(["α = 1%", "α = 5%"], {value: "α = 1%", label: "Significance level"})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="cl-dials pl-dials">${ins.mode}${ins.alpha}</div>`})
plPre  = [3, 5, 4, 1, 4, 8, 10, 15, 2, 9, 6, 3, 8, 11, 10]
plPost = [1, 6, 3, 2, 7, 3, 5, 8, 4, 7, 4, 2, 5, 7, 5]
plDif  = plPost.map((v, i) => v - plPre[i])
// H1: the cost fell, so both tests are left-tailed. The density reuses
// clLgam and the CDF clTcdf, both from #ci-lab.
plTpdf = (t, df) => Math.exp(clLgam((df + 1) / 2) - clLgam(df / 2) - 0.5 * Math.log(df * Math.PI)
  - (df + 1) / 2 * Math.log(1 + t * t / df))
plTests = {
  const n = plPre.length, est = d3.mean(plDif);
  const vPre = d3.variance(plPre), vPost = d3.variance(plPost), vDif = d3.variance(plDif);
  const sp2 = ((n - 1) * vPre + (n - 1) * vPost) / (2 * n - 2);
  const mk = (se, df) => ({se, df, t: est / se, p: clTcdf(est / se, df)});
  return {n, est, vPre, vPost, vDif,
    Paired: mk(Math.sqrt(vDif / n), n - 1),
    Independent: mk(Math.sqrt(sp2 * 2 / n), 2 * n - 2)};
}
{
  const T = plTests, paired = plIn.mode === "Paired", cur = T[plIn.mode];
  const a = plIn.alpha === "α = 1%" ? 0.01 : 0.05, crit = -clInv(t => clTcdf(t, cur.df))(1 - a);
  const style = ({fontSize: "14px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"});
  const title = s => Plot.text([s], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16});
  const neg = s => s.replace("-", "−");
  // Ties fan out sideways (0, -1, +1, -2, ...) so no dot hides another.
  const jit = vals => { const seen = {}; return vals.map(v => { const j = seen[v] = (seen[v] || 0) + 1; return ((j - 1) % 2 ? -1 : 1) * Math.ceil((j - 1) / 2) * 0.07; }); };
  const jPre = jit(plPre), jPost = jit(plPost), jDif = jit(plDif);
  const idx = d3.range(T.n), XD = 2.3;
  const names = new Map([[0, "Pre 2020"], [1, "Post 2020"], [XD, "Post − pre"]]);
  const data = Plot.plot({
    width: 470, height: 290, marginLeft: 34, marginBottom: 30, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [-0.5, XD + 0.6], ticks: [0, 1, XD], tickFormat: v => names.get(v), label: null, tickSize: 0},
    y: {domain: [-8, 16], ticks: [-8, -4, 0, 4, 8, 12, 16], tickFormat: v => neg(String(v)), label: null, insetTop: 18},
    marks: [
      title(`The ${T.n} firms, pre and post 2020`),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {x1: XD - 0.5, x2: XD + 0.5, stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      paired ? Plot.link(idx, {x1: i => jPre[i], y1: i => plPre[i], x2: i => 1 + jPost[i], y2: i => plPost[i], stroke: PPAL.dim, strokeWidth: 1.2}) : null,
      Plot.dot(idx, {x: i => jPre[i], y: i => plPre[i], r: 5, fill: PPAL.navy, fillOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.dot(idx, {x: i => 1 + jPost[i], y: i => plPost[i], r: 5, fill: PPAL.olive, fillOpacity: 0.7}),
      Plot.ruleY([d3.mean(plPre)], {x1: -0.3, x2: 0.3, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleY([d3.mean(plPost)], {x1: 0.7, x2: 1.3, stroke: PPAL.olive, strokeWidth: 3}),
      paired ? Plot.dot(idx, {x: i => XD + jDif[i], y: i => plDif[i], r: 5, fill: PPAL.orange, fillOpacity: 0.7}) : null,
      Plot.ruleY([T.est], {x1: XD - 0.3, x2: XD + 0.3, stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 3})
    ]
  });
  const G = d3.range(-4.5, 4.501, 0.05), tail = G.filter(t => t <= crit);
  const dist = Plot.plot({
    width: 470, height: 290, marginLeft: 12, marginRight: 12, marginBottom: 30, marginTop: 42, style,
    x: {domain: [-4.5, 4.5], label: null, tickSize: 4, tickFormat: v => neg(String(v))},
    y: {domain: [0, 0.42], axis: null, insetTop: 18},
    marks: [
      title(`The statistic against t with ${cur.df} df`),
      Plot.areaY(tail, {x: t => t, y: t => plTpdf(t, cur.df), fill: PPAL.brick, fillOpacity: 0.3}),
      Plot.lineY(G, {x: t => t, y: t => plTpdf(t, cur.df), stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      Plot.ruleX([crit], {y1: 0, y2: 0.3, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleX([cur.t], {y1: 0, y2: 0.36, stroke: "#3E3F3A", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.text([cur.t], {x: t => t, y: 0.36, dy: -10, dx: -12, textAnchor: "start", text: t => `t = ${neg(t.toFixed(3))}`,
        fill: "#3E3F3A", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700})
    ]
  });
  const m = v => neg(v.toFixed(3)), f4 = v => v.toFixed(4);
  const row = k => html`<span class="${k === plIn.mode ? "pl-on" : "pl-off"}">${k}: SE = ${m(T[k].se)}, t = ${m(T[k].t)}, p = ${f4(T[k].p)}</span>`;
  const rej = cur.p < a, cov2 = T.vPre + T.vPost - T.vDif;
  const why = paired
    ? `Firms that start high stay high, so the differences vary far less than the two groups put together: <b>s<sub>d</sub><sup>2</sup> = ${T.vDif.toFixed(2)}</b> against s<sub>pre</sub><sup>2</sup> + s<sub>post</sub><sup>2</sup> = ${(T.vPre + T.vPost).toFixed(2)}. Pairing removes twice the covariance, ${cov2.toFixed(2)}.`
    : `Treated as independent, the firm-to-firm spread stays in the standard error, <b>${m(T.Independent.se)}</b> instead of ${m(T.Paired.se)}. These are the same firms measured twice, so treating them as independent omits the pairing information.`;
  return html`<div class="cr-row pl-row">${data}${dist}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq cl-stats pl-stats">${row("Paired")}${row("Independent")}</div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">The p-value ${f4(cur.p)} is ${rej ? "below" : "above"} ${plIn.alpha}, so we <b>${rej ? "reject" : "do not reject"} H<sub>0</sub></b> (cut-off ${m(crit)}). ${why}</div>`;
}

rgAd = Array.from({length: rgRaw.length / 4}, (_, i) =>
  ({TV: rgRaw[4 * i], Radio: rgRaw[4 * i + 1], Newspaper: rgRaw[4 * i + 2], Sales: rgRaw[4 * i + 3]}))
rgMean = a => a.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) / a.length
// Simple least squares and every quantity of ISLR 3.1 from two columns.
// Checked against R's lm(), summary() and confint() to 4 decimals.
rgSimple = (x, y) => {
  const n = x.length, mx = rgMean(x), my = rgMean(y);
  let sxy = 0, sxx = 0, syy = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const dx = x[i] - mx, dy = y[i] - my; sxy += dx * dy; sxx += dx * dx; syy += dy * dy; }
  const b1 = sxy / sxx, b0 = my - b1 * mx, rss = syy - b1 * sxy, rse = Math.sqrt(rss / (n - 2)), se1 = rse / Math.sqrt(sxx);
  return {n, mx, my, sxy, sxx, b0, b1, rss, tss: syy, rse, se1, t1: b1 / se1,
          r: sxy / Math.sqrt(sxx * syy), r2: 1 - rss / syy, adj: 1 - (rss / (n - 2)) / (syy / (n - 1))};
}
// Multiple least squares (ISLR 3.2): the normal equations, inverted by
// Gauss-Jordan, so the standard errors come from the same inverse.
rgOls = names => {
  const n = rgAd.length, k = names.length + 1, y = rgAd.map(d => d.Sales);
  const X = rgAd.map(d => [1, ...names.map(v => d[v])]);
  const A = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) => [
    ...Array.from({length: k}, (_, j) => X.reduce((s, row) => s + row[i] * row[j], 0)),
    ...Array.from({length: k}, (_, j) => +(i === j))]);
  for (let c = 0; c < k; c++) {
    let piv = c;
    for (let r = c + 1; r < k; r++) if (Math.abs(A[r][c]) > Math.abs(A[piv][c])) piv = r;
    [A[c], A[piv]] = [A[piv], A[c]];
    const d = A[c][c];
    for (let j = 0; j < 2 * k; j++) A[c][j] /= d;
    for (let r = 0; r < k; r++) if (r !== c) { const f = A[r][c]; for (let j = 0; j < 2 * k; j++) A[r][j] -= f * A[c][j]; }
  }
  const inv = A.map(row => row.slice(k));
  const xty = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) => X.reduce((s, row, m) => s + row[i] * y[m], 0));
  const b = inv.map(row => row.reduce((s, v, j) => s + v * xty[j], 0));
  const my = rgMean(y), df = n - k;
  const rss = X.reduce((s, row, m) => s + (y[m] - row.reduce((a, v, j) => a + v * b[j], 0)) ** 2, 0);
  const tss = y.reduce((s, v) => s + (v - my) ** 2, 0), s2 = rss / df;
  const se = inv.map((row, i) => Math.sqrt(s2 * row[i]));
  return {names: ["Intercept", ...names], b, se, t: b.map((v, i) => v / se[i]), n, k, df, rss, tss,
          rse: Math.sqrt(s2), r2: 1 - rss / tss, adj: 1 - (rss / df) / (tss / (n - 1)), F: ((tss - rss) / (k - 1)) / s2};
}
// p-values from the exact t and F distributions (clTcdf, clIbeta: section 05).
rgP2 = (t, df) => 2 * clTcdf(-Math.abs(t), df)
rgFp = (F, d1, d2) => clIbeta(d2 / 2, d1 / 2, d2 / (d2 + d1 * F))
rgPfmt = p => p < 0.0001 ? "< 0.0001" : p.toFixed(4)
rgPeq = p => `p ${p < 0.0001 ? "" : "= "}${rgPfmt(p)}`
rgN = (v, k = 4) => v.toLocaleString("en-GB", {minimumFractionDigits: k, maximumFractionDigits: k}).replace("-", "−")
// A negative factor in a product goes in brackets: "6.47 − (−0.56) × 7.47".
rgNp = (v, k = 4) => v < 0 ? `(${rgN(v, k)})` : rgN(v, k)
rgCol = name => rgAd.map(d => d[name])
rgTV = rgSimple(rgCol("TV"), rgCol("Sales"))
rgStyle = ({fontSize: "14px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif", color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
rgTitle = s => Plot.text([s], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -30, text: d => d, fill: PPAL.navy, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16})
{
  const fit = rgSimple(rgCol(rgSx), rgCol("Sales")), hi = d3.max(rgCol(rgSx));
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: 1000, height: 280, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [0, hi * 1.02], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, 28], label: null, ticks: [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25], tickSize: 4},
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(rgAd, {x: rgSx, y: "Sales", r: 3.5, fill: PPAL.soft, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
      Plot.line([0, hi], {x: d => d, y: d => fit.b0 + fit.b1 * d, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 3}),
      rgTitle(`Sales (1000s of units) against the ${rgSx} budget ($1000s)`)
    ]
  });
  const pct = v => `${(100 * v).toFixed(1)}%`;
  const say = rgSx === "Newspaper"
    ? `Newspaper has the weakest correlation with sales: r = ${rgN(fit.r, 3)}. The fitted line has a positive slope and explains <b>${pct(fit.r2)}</b> of the variation in sales. The multiple regression example examines how this relationship changes when radio is included.`
    : `${rgSx} has r = ${rgN(fit.r, 3)}, so the line explains <b>R² = r² = ${pct(fit.r2)}</b> of the variation in sales. Each extra $1,000 on ${rgSx === "TV" ? "TV" : "radio"} goes with about <b>${(1000 * fit.b1).toFixed(1)} more units</b> sold.`;
  return html`${chart}
  <div class="ojs-eq rg-stats">
    <span>Sales = ${rgN(fit.b0)} + ${rgN(fit.b1)} × ${rgSx}</span>
    <span>r = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(fit.r, 3)}</span></span>
    <span>R² = ${rgN(fit.r2, 3)}</span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${say}</div>`;
}

Testing the population correlation

Under \(H_0\colon \rho = 0\), \(t = \frac{r\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}\) follows Student’s \(t\) with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom. The defaults are \(r = 0.33\) over 24 months.

viewof rgCin = Inputs.form({
  r: Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.33, step: 0.01, label: html`Correlation <i style="text-transform: none">r</i>`}),
  n: Inputs.range([5, 200], {value: 24, step: 1, label: html`Sample size <i style="text-transform: none">n</i>`}),
  alt: Inputs.radio(["ρ > 0", "ρ < 0", "ρ ≠ 0"], {value: "ρ > 0", label: "Alternative"}),
  alpha: Inputs.radio(["10%", "5%", "1%"], {value: "5%", label: html`Level <i style="text-transform: none">α</i>`})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="rg-dials">${ins.r}${ins.n}</div><div class="rg-dials rg-dials-2">${ins.alt}${ins.alpha}</div>`})
{
  const {r, n, alt} = rgCin, df = n - 2, a = parseFloat(rgCin.alpha) / 100;
  const t = r * Math.sqrt(df) / Math.sqrt(1 - r * r);
  const crit = clInv(x => clTcdf(x, df))(alt === "ρ ≠ 0" ? 1 - a / 2 : 1 - a);
  const p = alt === "ρ > 0" ? 1 - clTcdf(t, df) : alt === "ρ < 0" ? clTcdf(t, df) : rgP2(t, df);
  const inR = x => alt === "ρ > 0" ? x >= crit : alt === "ρ < 0" ? x <= -crit : Math.abs(x) >= crit;
  const reject = inR(t);
  const dens = x => Math.exp(clLgam((df + 1) / 2) - clLgam(df / 2) - 0.5 * Math.log(df * Math.PI) - (df + 1) / 2 * Math.log(1 + x * x / df));
  const xs = d3.range(-6, 6.001, 0.02).map(x => ({x, y: dens(x)}));
  const cuts = alt === "ρ > 0" ? [crit] : alt === "ρ < 0" ? [-crit] : [-crit, crit];
  const tc = Math.max(-6, Math.min(6, t));
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: 1000, height: 210, marginLeft: 12, marginRight: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [-6, 6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {axis: null, domain: [0, 0.42], insetTop: 18},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(xs, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: PPAL.dim, fillOpacity: 0.3}),
      Plot.areaY(xs, {x: "x", y: d => inR(d.x) ? d.y : NaN, fill: PPAL.brick, fillOpacity: 0.45}),
      Plot.line(xs, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleX(cuts, {stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleX([tc], {stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.text([tc], {x: d => d, y: 0.36, text: () => `t = ${rgN(t, 2)}${Math.abs(t) > 6 ? " (off the axis)" : ""}`, dx: tc > 3 ? -8 : 8,
        textAnchor: tc > 3 ? "end" : "start", fill: PPAL.orange, fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 16, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 6}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      rgTitle(`Student's t with ${df} degrees of freedom; the red tail is the rejection region`)
    ]
  });
  const word = {"ρ > 0": "greater than zero", "ρ < 0": "less than zero", "ρ ≠ 0": "different from zero"}[alt];
  return html`${chart}
  <div class="ojs-eq rg-stats">
    <span>t = <span class="rate">${rgN(t, 4)}</span></span>
    <span>Critical value ${alt === "ρ ≠ 0" ? "±" : alt === "ρ < 0" ? "−" : ""}${rgN(crit, 4)}</span>
    <span>${rgPeq(p)}</span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${reject
    ? html`The statistic t = ${rgN(t, 2)} falls in the rejection region, so we <b>reject H₀</b> at the ${rgCin.alpha} level: the correlation is ${word} (${rgPeq(p)}).`
    : html`The statistic t = ${rgN(t, 2)} is not in the rejection region, so we <b>fail to reject H₀</b> at the ${rgCin.alpha} level (${rgPeq(p)}). A correlation of ${rgN(r, 2)} from only ${n} pairs could be chance.`}</div>`;
}

Finding the Least-Squares Line

Each line gives residuals \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\). Least squares picks the line with the smallest \(\text{RSS} = \sum e_i^2\) (ISLR Figures 3.1 and 3.2). Find it with the sliders.

viewof rgLin = Inputs.form({
  b0: Inputs.range([5, 9], {value: 8.5, step: 0.01, label: html`Intercept <i style="text-transform: none">β₀</i>`}),
  b1: Inputs.range([0.03, 0.065], {value: 0.035, step: 0.0005, label: html`Slope <i style="text-transform: none">β₁</i>`})
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="rg-dials">${ins.b0}${ins.b1}</div>`})
rgSums = {
  const x = rgCol("TV"), y = rgCol("Sales"), s = f => x.reduce((a, _, i) => a + f(x[i], y[i]), 0);
  return {n: x.length, sx: s(u => u), sy: s((u, v) => v), sxx: s(u => u * u), sxy: s((u, v) => u * v), syy: s((u, v) => v * v)};
}
rgRSS = (b0, b1) => { const S = rgSums;
  return S.syy - 2 * b0 * S.sy - 2 * b1 * S.sxy + S.n * b0 * b0 + 2 * b0 * b1 * S.sx + b1 * b1 * S.sxx; }
{
  const {b0, b1} = rgLin, rss = rgRSS(b0, b1), min = rgTV.rss;
  const scatter = Plot.plot({
    width: 500, height: 270, marginLeft: 36, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [0, 300], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, 28], label: null, ticks: [0, 10, 20], tickSize: 4},
    marks: [
      Plot.link(rgAd, {x1: "TV", x2: "TV", y1: "Sales", y2: d => b0 + b1 * d.TV, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeOpacity: 0.55, strokeWidth: 1.2}),
      Plot.dot(rgAd, {x: "TV", y: "Sales", r: 3, fill: PPAL.soft, fillOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.line([0, 300], {x: d => d, y: d => b0 + b1 * d, stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 3}),
      rgTitle("Your line and its residuals")
    ]
  });
  const contour = Plot.plot({
    width: 480, height: 270, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 40, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [5, 9], label: "Intercept β₀", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none", tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0.03, 0.065], label: "Slope β₁", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none", tickSize: 4, ticks: 4},
    marks: [
      Plot.contour({x1: 5, x2: 9, y1: 0.03, y2: 0.065, value: rgRSS, pixelSize: 3,
        thresholds: [2150, 2200, 2300, 2500, 3000, 4000, 6000, 10000, 16000], stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeOpacity: 0.35, fill: "none"}),
      Plot.dot([rgTV], {x: "b0", y: "b1", symbol: "plus", r: 7, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([rgLin], {x: "b0", y: "b1", r: 6, fill: PPAL.orange, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      rgTitle("RSS for every intercept and slope")
    ]
  });
  const over = rss / min - 1;
  return html`<div class="cr-row">${scatter}${contour}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq rg-stats">
    <span>Your RSS = <span class="rate">${rgN(rss, 1)}</span></span>
    <span>Least-squares RSS = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(min, 1)}</span> <span class="na-note">At (${rgN(rgTV.b0)}, ${rgN(rgTV.b1)})</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb ${over < 0.005 ? "quiz-ok" : ""}">${over < 0.005
    ? html`Within 0.5% of the minimum: this is the least-squares line, intercept ${rgN(rgTV.b0, 2)} and slope ${rgN(rgTV.b1)}. No other line leaves a smaller total of squared residuals.`
    : html`Your RSS is <b>${(100 * over).toFixed(1)}% above</b> the minimum. Move the orange dot towards the navy cross: the contours are levels of RSS, and the valley is long and narrow because a steeper slope can be traded for a lower intercept.`}</div>`;
}

The Least-Squares Estimates

Setting the derivatives of RSS to zero gives the line in closed form. Select a data set to calculate the estimates and a prediction.

\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2}, \qquad \widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar y - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar x\]

rgSets = ({
  "Advertising: sales on TV": {x: rgCol("TV"), y: rgCol("Sales"), lo: 0, hi: 400, x0: 100, step: 1,
    say: b1 => `Each extra $1,000 of TV budget goes with ${(1000 * b1).toFixed(1)} more units sold.`},
  "Exercise 2: Y on X": {x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], y: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128], lo: 0, hi: 10, x0: 5, step: 0.5,
    say: b1 => `A one-unit increase in X goes with an increase of ${rgN(b1, 2)} in Y.`},
  "Exercise 3: cost of debt on sales": {x: [15, 4, 12, 17, 13, 3, 5, 1, 14, 1, 6, 9, 8, 2, 2],
    y: [2, 6, 3, 2, 4, 7, 9, 14, 3, 7, 4, 6, 7, 12, 11], lo: 0, hi: 25, x0: 10, step: 0.5,
    say: b1 => `Each extra £1 million of sales goes with a ${rgN(-b1, 2)} percentage-point lower cost of debt.`}
})
viewof rgFset = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(rgSets), {value: "Advertising: sales on TV", label: "Data"})
viewof rgFx0 = Inputs.range([rgSets[rgFset].lo, rgSets[rgFset].hi], {value: rgSets[rgFset].x0, step: rgSets[rgFset].step, label: html`Predict at <i style="text-transform: none">x</i>`})
{
  const D = rgSets[rgFset], f = rgSimple(D.x, D.y), yhat = f.b0 + f.b1 * rgFx0;
  const lo = d3.min(D.x), hi = d3.max(D.x), inside = rgFx0 >= lo && rgFx0 <= hi;
  const bar = v => html`<span class="cl-bar">${v}</span>`, hat = v => html`<span class="rg-hat">${v}</span>`;
  return html`<div class="ojs-eq cr-eqs rg-eqs">
    <span>${bar("x")}, ${bar("y")}</span><span>= ${rgN(f.mx)}, ${rgN(f.my)}</span>
    <span>${hat("β")}₁</span><span>= ${rgN(f.sxy, 2)} / ${rgN(f.sxx, 2)} = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(f.b1)}</span></span>
    <span>${hat("β")}₀</span><span>= ${rgN(f.my)} − ${rgNp(f.b1)} × ${rgN(f.mx)} = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(f.b0)}</span></span>
    <span>${hat("y")}</span><span>= ${rgN(f.b0)} + ${rgNp(f.b1)} × ${rgFx0} = <span class="${inside ? "rate" : "miss"}">${rgN(yhat)}</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb ${inside ? "" : "quiz-no"}">${D.say(f.b1)} ${inside
    ? html`At x = ${rgFx0}, inside the data's range ${lo} to ${hi}, the line predicts <b>${rgN(yhat, 2)}</b>.`
    : html`But x = ${rgFx0} lies outside the data's range ${lo} to ${hi}: predicting there is <b>extrapolation</b>, and nothing in the data says the line still holds.`}</div>`;
}

How Accurate Is the Slope?

Resample the 200 markets with replacement and refit. The spread of the resampled slopes is what \(\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\) measures (ISLR Figure 3.3, Table 3.1).

viewof rgBin = Inputs.form({
  c: Inputs.range([0, 0.06], {value: 0, step: 0.001, label: html`Test H₀: <i style="text-transform: none">β₁</i> =`}),
  again: Inputs.button("New resamples")
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="rg-dials">${ins.c}${ins.again}</div>`})
// 1,000 bootstrap resamples, seeded from the button so moving the null value
// keeps the same resamples. Their sd of the slope lands near the formula SE
// (about 0.0028 against 0.0027).
rgBoot = {
  const rnd = d3.randomLcg(((rgBin.again + 1) * 0.6180339887) % 1), x = rgCol("TV"), y = rgCol("Sales");
  const n = x.length, bx = new Array(n), by = new Array(n);
  return Array.from({length: 1000}, () => {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const j = Math.floor(rnd() * n); bx[i] = x[j]; by[i] = y[j]; }
    const f = rgSimple(bx, by);
    return {b0: f.b0, b1: f.b1};
  });
}
{
  const f = rgTV, c = rgBin.c, lo = f.b1 - 2 * f.se1, hi = f.b1 + 2 * f.se1;
  const t = (f.b1 - c) / f.se1, p = rgP2(t, f.n - 2), inside = c >= lo && c <= hi;
  const lines = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 250, marginLeft: 36, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [0, 300], label: null, tickSize: 4},
    y: {domain: [0, 28], label: null, ticks: [0, 10, 20], tickSize: 4},
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(rgAd, {x: "TV", y: "Sales", r: 2.5, fill: PPAL.soft, fillOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.link(rgBoot.slice(0, 100), {x1: () => 0, x2: () => 300, y1: d => d.b0, y2: d => d.b0 + 300 * d.b1, stroke: "#9FB6CC", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
      Plot.line([0, 300], {x: d => d, y: d => f.b0 + f.b1 * d, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 3}),
      rgTitle("A hundred of the 1,000 resampled lines")
    ]
  });
  const hist = Plot.plot({
    width: 490, height: 250, marginLeft: 12, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 42, style: rgStyle,
    x: {domain: [-0.002, 0.062], label: null, tickSize: 4, ticks: [0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06]},
    y: {axis: null, insetTop: 18},
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(rgBoot, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "b1", thresholds: d3.range(-0.002, 0.0621, 0.0005), fill: "#9FB6CC"})),
      Plot.ruleX([lo, hi], {stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
      Plot.ruleX([c], {stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim}),
      rgTitle("Slopes of the 1,000 resamples")
    ]
  });
  const sdBoot = d3.deviation(rgBoot, d => d.b1);
  return html`<div class="cr-row">${lines}${hist}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq rg-stats">
    <span>SE = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(f.se1, 5)}</span> <span class="na-note">(resampled sd ${rgN(sdBoot, 5)})</span></span>
    <span>95% CI = [${rgN(lo)}, ${rgN(hi)}]</span>
    <span>t = <span class="rate">${rgN(t, 2)}</span></span>
    <span>${rgPeq(p)}</span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${inside
    ? html`The value ${c} lies inside the interval β̂₁ ± 2·SE, so the test does not reject it: t = ${rgN(t, 2)}, ${rgPeq(p)}. The interval is the set of null values the test does not reject at 5%.`
    : html`The value ${c} lies outside the interval β̂₁ ± 2·SE, so we <b>reject H₀</b>: t = (${rgN(f.b1, 5)} − ${c}) / ${rgN(f.se1, 5)} = ${rgN(t, 2)}, ${rgPeq(p)}.${c === 0 ? " TV advertising is related to sales, as in ISLR Table 3.1." : ""}`}</div>`;
}

How Well Does the Line Fit?

Three numbers summarise the fit of sales on TV (ISLR 3.1.3). The first is in the units of \(y\); the other two are shares of the variation in \(y\).

RSE

\(\text{RSE} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}}\)

The residual standard error is about thousand units, % of average sales.

R²

\(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}}\)

TV explains % of the variation in sales.

Adjusted R²

\(\bar R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{\text{RSS}/(n-k-1)}{\text{TSS}/(n-1)}\)

Equal to here. It accounts for the number of predictors, \(k\), when comparing models.

In simple regression \(R^2 = r^2\): the correlation of sales and TV is , and ² = . Adding a predictor never lowers \(R^2\), so adjusted \(R^2\) accounts for model size when comparing fits.

Simple Versus Multiple Regression

Tick the media to include. Each coefficient is the change in sales per $1,000 on that medium, holding the other ticked media fixed (ISLR 3.2).

viewof rgMx = Inputs.checkbox(["TV", "Radio", "Newspaper"], {value: ["TV", "Radio", "Newspaper"], label: "Predictors"})
{
  const vars = ["TV", "Radio", "Newspaper"].filter(v => rgMx.includes(v));
  const cols = ["TV", "Radio", "Newspaper", "Sales"];
  const cor = (a, b) => rgSimple(rgCol(a), rgCol(b)).r;
  const corTable = html`<table class="rg-table rg-cor">
    <thead><tr><th></th>${cols.map(c => html`<th>${c}</th>`)}</tr></thead>
    <tbody>${cols.map(a => html`<tr><th>${a}</th>${cols.map(b => html`<td class=${(a === "Radio" && b === "Newspaper") || (a === "Newspaper" && b === "Radio") ? "ct-top" : ""}>${rgN(cor(a, b), 2)}</td>`)}</tr>`)}</tbody>
  </table>`;
  if (!vars.length) return html`<div class="rg-row"><div class="quiz-fb">Tick at least one medium to fit a model.</div>${corTable}</div>`;
  const m = rgOls(vars), pF = rgFp(m.F, m.k - 1, m.df);
  const coef = html`<table class="rg-table">
    <thead><tr><th></th><th>Coefficient</th><th>Std. error</th><th>t</th><th>P-value</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>${m.names.map((nm, i) => html`<tr class=${nm === "Newspaper" ? "rg-news" : ""}><th>${nm}</th><td>${rgN(m.b[i])}</td><td>${rgN(m.se[i])}</td><td>${rgN(m.t[i], 2)}</td><td>${rgPfmt(rgP2(m.t[i], m.df))}</td></tr>`)}</tbody>
  </table>`;
  const ni = m.names.indexOf("Newspaper"), np = ni > 0 ? rgP2(m.t[ni], m.df) : null;
  const m2 = ni < 0 ? rgOls([...vars, "Newspaper"]) : null;
  const say = ni < 0
    ? html`F = ${rgN(m.F, 1)} (${rgPeq(pF)}): at least one ticked medium is related to sales. Adding newspaper would raise R² from ${rgN(m.r2, 5)} to ${rgN(m2.r2, 5)}, but ${m2.adj < m.adj ? "lower" : "raise"} adjusted R² from ${rgN(m.adj, 5)} to ${rgN(m2.adj, 5)}.`
    : vars.includes("Radio")
      ? html`Holding radio${vars.includes("TV") ? " and TV" : ""} fixed, newspaper's coefficient is <b>${rgN(m.b[ni])}</b> (${rgPeq(np)}): no effect of its own. On its own it looked useful only because markets that spend on radio also spend on newspapers (r = ${rgN(cor("Radio", "Newspaper"), 2)}).`
      : html`Without radio, newspaper's coefficient is <b>${rgN(m.b[ni])}</b> (${rgPeq(np)}). It picks up radio's effect, because the two budgets are correlated (r = ${rgN(cor("Radio", "Newspaper"), 2)}): this is <b>omitted variable bias</b>. Include radio to compare the coefficient estimates.`;
  return html`<div class="rg-row">${coef}${corTable}</div>
  <div class="ojs-eq rg-stats">
    <span>R² = ${rgN(m.r2, 3)}</span>
    <span>Adjusted R² = ${rgN(m.adj, 3)}</span>
    <span>RSE = ${rgN(m.rse, 2)}</span>
    <span>F = <span class="cl-navy">${rgN(m.F, 1)}</span> <span class="na-note">(${rgPeq(pF)})</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="quiz-fb">${say}</div>`;
}
